docs.text:
BayesEoR is a physically motivated forward-modelling framework for Bayesian recovery of the 21-cm power spectrum from interferometric visibilities. Every contribution to the data is modelled jointly and propagated through the instrument response, so the recovered power spectrum and Bayesian evidence reflect their combined uncertainty.

This version is written in JAX and runs on CPU or GPU, with optional distributed GPU linear algebra through JAXMg.

docs.title: How BayesEoR works
docs.text:
In interferometric visibilities, the 21-cm signal is a faint, low signal-to-noise contribution, buried beneath Galactic and extragalactic foregrounds roughly \(10^4\)–\(10^5\) times brighter. The chromatic response of the instrument then maps both into highly degenerate structures, making its extraction a formidable inference problem. Any foreground structure a model fails to describe can be absorbed by the signal and mistaken for a detection, so both must be inferred together within a joint posterior, given by Bayes' theorem:

\[ P(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\boldsymbol d,\mathcal M) = \frac{\mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol\theta,\mathcal M)\, \pi(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal M)} {\mathcal Z(\boldsymbol d\mid\mathcal M)}. \]

Unlike most other approaches, BayesEoR evaluates the Bayesian evidence, \(\mathcal Z\), alongside the posterior. Comparing evidences between models with and without a 21-cm component quantifies the statistical significance of a detection, and allows the framework to be rigorously validated against spurious detections.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: The quickest way to get started is to run one of the two examples. Each infers a 21-cm power spectrum from a small simulated observation, and takes a few minutes on a laptop.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Create and activate the CPU environment, as described in installation:

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate bayeseor

docs.title: 2. Run an example
docs.text:
From the repository root, run either example:

21-cm only21-cm and foregrounds 
python -m examples.eor.run --sample

Infers the power spectrum of a simulated 21-cm signal, with no foregrounds. See 21-cm only.

python -m examples.eor_fgs.run --sample

Adds bright foregrounds, compresses them into a KL reduced basis, and infers the power spectrum jointly. See 21-cm and foregrounds.

Without --sample, each example stops after setup, which is a quick check that the installation works.

docs.title: 3. Look at the results
docs.text: Each example writes its power-spectrum and posterior figure to its plots/ folder, for example examples/eor/plots/power_spectrum_and_posteriors.png, and its full outputs under outputs/. See posterior analysis for reading them yourself.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
To analyse your own data, start from an example's config.yaml and change its settings:

  • Data: point it at your visibilities and describe the instrument and observation.
  • Model: choose the EoR and foreground fields and resolution.
  • Inference: set the power-spectrum priors and run the sampler.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Through JAX and JAXMg, BayesEoR scales from a single desktop computer to multi-GPU HPC clusters. The models, likelihood and sampler are the same in every case; only the linear-algebra backend changes.

Clone the repository, then create the environment matching your system:

git clone https://github.com/JacobTutt/BayesEoR-JAX.git
cd BayesEoR-JAX

Desktop or CPU workstation

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate bayeseor

Linux NVIDIA GPU cluster

conda env create -f environment-hpc.yml
conda activate bayeseor-hpc

Note

Conda is used to install the native MultiNest library alongside its Python interface, PyMultiNest. pip install pymultinest alone installs only the wrapper. We recommend Miniforge.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Both environments use Python 3.12 or newer and JAX 0.11.1 or newer. On GPU clusters, the dense linear algebra is distributed across devices with JAXMg, which is built on NVIDIA's cuSOLVERMp, so the GPU environment is restricted to NVIDIA systems. It installs jaxmg[cuda12], which provides CUDA-enabled JAX; see the JAXMg installation guide for supported GPUs and drivers.

docs.title: Construction and KL reduction
docs.text:
Build the operators on disk in CPU blocks, compress the foregrounds into a KL reduced basis, and precompute the likelihood products.

\[ \mathbf A=\mathbf N^{-1/2}\mathbf T\,\mathbf\Sigma^{1/2}=\mathbf U\mathbf S\mathbf V^\dagger, \qquad \mathbf T_r=\mathbf N^{1/2}\mathbf U_r\mathbf S_r \]

Construction API

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
Evaluate the marginalised likelihood and MAP coefficients, and sample the power-spectrum posterior.

\[ \mathbf\Sigma(\boldsymbol\varphi)=\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\mathbf T +\mathbf\Psi^{-1}(\boldsymbol\varphi), \qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol b}=\mathbf\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\boldsymbol d \]

Inference API

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Read weighted MultiNest chains, summarise each \(k\) bin and plot the results.

Analysis API

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
DataContainer reads one or more MultiNest runs with their setup metadata, and summarises the posterior on \(\Delta^2_{21}(k)\) in each bin. The plotting functions take a DataContainer and return Matplotlib figures and axes. See posterior analysis for a guide.

from bayeseor_jax import DataContainer
from bayeseor_jax.analyze import plot_power_spectra_and_posteriors

dc = DataContainer(["outputs/multinest"])
fig, (power_ax, posterior_axes) = plot_power_spectra_and_posteriors(dc)

None

Decompose and truncate A, then save T_fg,r = N^1/2 U_r S_r.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default weighted_operator_path Path or str

Saved complex128 matrix A = N^-1/2 T_fg Sigma_q^1/2, shape (n_visibility, n_foreground_coefficient), in time/frequency/baseline row order. Prior and noise weighting must already have been applied.

required ninv_path Path or str

required output_path Path or str

Shared destination, normally T_fg_reduced.npy. Also saves singular values to .singular_values.npy and diagnostics to .svd.json. required f float

Maximum discarded RMS as a fraction of thermal-noise RMS, averaged over the original visibility vector. Defaults to 0.1; see select_foreground_rank for the precise criterion.

0.1 tile_size int

Positive JAXMG square tile width, default 128. Unused on CPU.

128

Returns:

Type Description Path

Completed complex128 operator, shape (n_visibility, retained_rank), ready for joint assembly with a standard-normal foreground prior.

Notes

On CPU, native JAX computes an unpadded, thin SVD on one device in one process. The input, thin singular-vector matrices and solver workspace must fit in local RAM. This path requires neither CUDA nor JAXMG.

On GPU, every process calls together, with one GPU per process and shared storage. Only local shards are read from disk; zero padding permits the distributed JAXMG GESVD. Full U is never gathered, and Vh is not computed. This is a dense SVD: the input, U and solver workspace must fit the allocated GPUs. Padding is excluded from the output and the RMS normalisation.

This function always computes its requested product, independently of setup and cache policy. It neither constructs A nor changes the inference prior. Existing outputs are replaced only after successful computation. The JAX backend selects the implementation; a GPU solver failure does not trigger a CPU fallback. Neither path uses approximate/randomised decomposition.

select_foreground_rank(singular_values, n_vis, f=0.1)

Find the smallest rank meeting the discarded prior-predictive RMS limit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default singular_values array - like

Non-negative singular values of A = N^-1/2 T_fg Sigma_q^1/2, ordered from largest to smallest, with modes introduced by padding excluded.

required n_vis int

required f float

The criterion is epsilon(r) = sqrt(sum(s[r:]**2) / n_vis) <= f. This is an average in noise-whitened visibility space, not a bound on each sample or on each realisation. The foreground prior is not applied a second time.

preprocess_uvdata(filepath, antenna_selection='cross', bl_cutoff=None, freq_idx_min=None, freq_min=None, freq_center=None, n_freqs_select=None, jd_idx_min=None, jd_min=None, jd_center=None, n_times_select=None, form_pi=True, pi_norm=1.0, pol='xx', redundant_avg=False, uniform_redundancy=False, calc_noise=False, return_uvd=False, save_vis=False, save_model=False, save_dir='./', clobber=False)

Read visibility data from disk and form a one-dimensional data vector.

This function loads a pyuvdata-compatible file containing visibilities for a set of baselines (Nbls), times (Ntimes), and frequencies (Nfreqs) and forms a one-dimensional data vector with shape (2*Nbls * Ntimes * Nfreqs,) and an accompanying instrument model of baseline coordinates in metres and a redundancy model (when averaging redundant baselines). The factor of two comes from appending conjugate visibilities at reversed baselines (u, v, w) -> (-u, -v, -w). These are redundant copies of the measurements, not independent observations. Time is the slowest axis, frequency next, and baseline fastest.

Optionally, if calc_noise is True, a noise vector is also produced. The noise is estimated by differencing visibilities at even and odd time steps per baseline and frequency.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default filepath Path or str

Path read by pyuvdata (normally UVH5, UVFITS or a Measurement Set). Unlike get_vis_data, this lower-level function delegates format detection directly to UVData.read. Input units must be Jy or K sr.

required antenna_selection str

Antenna downselect string. This determines what baselines to keep in the data vector. Please see pyuvdata.UVData.select for more details. Defaults to 'cross' (cross-correlation baselines only).

'cross' bl_cutoff Quantity or float

Cutoff on sqrt(u2 + v2), in metres if not a Quantity. Defaults to None (keep all baselines).

None freq_idx_min int

Minimum frequency channel index to keep in the data vector. Defaults to None (keep all frequencies).

None freq_min Quantity or float

Minimum frequency to keep in the data vector in Hertz if not a Quantity. All frequencies greater than or equal to freq_min will be kept, unless n_freqs_select is specified. Defaults to None (keep all frequencies).

None freq_center Quantity or float

Central frequency, in Hertz if not a Quantity, around which n_freqs_select frequencies will be kept in the data vector. n_freqs_select must also be passed, otherwise an error is raised. Defaults to None (keep all frequencies).

None n_freqs_select int

Number of frequencies to keep starting from freq_idx_min, the channel corresponding to freq_min, or around freq_center. Defaults to None (keep all frequencies).

None jd_idx_min int

Minimum time index to keep in the data vector. Defaults to None (keep all times).

None jd_min Time or float

Minimum time to keep in the data vector as a Julian date if not a Time. Defaults to None (keep all times).

None jd_center Time or float

Central time, as a Julian date if not a Time, around which n_times_select times will be kept in the data vector. n_times_select must also be passed, otherwise an error is raised. Defaults to None (keep all times).

None n_times_select int

Number of times to keep starting from jd_idx_min, the time corresponding to jd_min or around jd_center. Defaults to None (keep all times).

None form_pi bool

Form pseudo-Stokes I visibilities. Otherwise, use the polarization specified by pol. Defaults to True.

True pi_norm float

Normalization, N, used in forming pseudo-Stokes I from XX and YY via pI = N * (XX + YY). Defaults to 1.0.

1.0 pol str

Case-insensitive polarization string. Used only if form_pi is False. Defaults to 'xx'.

'xx' redundant_avg bool

Redundantly average the data. Defaults to False.

False uniform_redundancy bool

Force the redundancy model to be uniform. Defaults to False.

False calc_noise bool

Calculate a noise estimate from the visibilities via differencing adjacent times per baseline and frequency. Defaults to False.

False return_uvd bool

Return the preprocessed UVData object. Defaults to False.

False save_vis bool

Write visibility vector to disk in save_dir. If calc_noise is True, also save the noise vector. Defaults to False.

False save_model bool

Write instrument model (antenna pairs, (u, v, w) sampling, and redundancy model) to disk in save_dir. Defaults to False.

False save_dir Path or str

Output directory if save_vis or save_model is True. Defaults to './'.

'./' clobber bool

Clobber files on disk if they exist. Defaults to False.

False

Returns:

Name Type Description vis ndarray

Complex visibility vector in mK sr, shape (2NblsNfreqs*Ntimes,).

antpairs list of tuple

List of antenna pair tuples corresponding to the (u, v, w) coordinates in uvws, in identical order, with length (2*Nbls).

uvws ndarray

Baseline coordinates in metres, shape (Ntimes, 2*Nbls, 3). The ordering of the Nbls axis matches the ordering of the baselines in vis.

redundancy ndarray

Redundancy model containing the number of baselines averaged within a redundant baseline group, shape (Ntimes, 2*Nbls, 1).

noise ndarray or None

Estimated noise vector with shape (2NblsNfreqs*Ntimes,). Returned as None when calc_noise is False.

uvd UVData or None

Preprocessed UVData object. Returned only if return_uvd is True.

Notes

This path assumes a common set of baselines at every selected time and unprojected drift-scan geometry. Fully flagged baselines are removed, but individual flagged samples are not masked or assigned zero weight here. The returned UVData data array has been converted to mK sr; its original vis_units label is not updated. Use the returned vector for inference.

docs.text:
Supply the beam weights multiplying image-domain sky brightness.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default beam_type str

Supported beam types are:

  • uniform: unit power response above the horizon (the default).
  • gaussian: Gaussian profile with a specified angular width or an aperture-derived, frequency-dependent width.
  • airy: Airy power pattern for a circular aperture.
  • gausscosine: Gaussian profile modulated by a cosine-squared response.
  • taperairy: Airy power pattern multiplied by a Gaussian taper.
  • tanhairy: Airy power pattern multiplied by a hyperbolic-tangent taper.
  • A beamfits file path: an arbitrary tabulated beam loaded through pyuvdata.UVBeam and interpolated onto the sky-pixel directions and observing frequencies. Both HEALPix and azimuth/zenith-angle beam grids are supported; pol selects the polarisation and freq_interp_kind selects the frequency interpolation method (cubic by default).
None peak_amp float

Peak power-response amplitude for Gaussian-based profiles. Defaults to 1.0; the uniform and untapered Airy profiles have unit peak.

1.0 fwhm_deg float

Full width at half maximum in degrees. Gaussian-based profiles use this width when supplied, otherwise deriving a width from diam.

None diam float

Antenna (aperture) diameter in meters. Used if beam_type is 'airy'.

None cosfreq float

Cosine frequency in inverse radians. Used if beam_type is 'gausscosine'.

None tanh_freq float

Exponential frequency (rate parameter) in inverse radians. Used if beam_type is 'tanhairy'.

None tanh_sl_red float

Fractional suppression of the Airy power response far from zenith. Used if beam_type is 'tanhairy'.

None pol str

Polarization string. Used only if beam_type is a UVBeam file path. Defaults to 'xx'.

'xx' freq_interp_kind str

Frequency interpolation kind from scipy.interpolate.interp1d. Defaults to 'cubic'.

'cubic' Notes

Analytic profiles or an interpolated UVBeam power model are evaluated at each pixel's topocentric direction and observing frequency. get_beam_vals returns the diagonal entries of the primary-beam operator; it does not allocate a dense diagonal matrix.

required_healpix_nside(longest_baseline_m: float, highest_frequency_hz: float, *, samples_per_fringe: float = 2.0) -> int

Estimate the HEALPix resolution needed to sample the shortest fringe.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default longest_baseline_m float

Largest physical baseline length in metres, finite and non-negative. Use the full three-dimensional length, not just its uv projection.

required highest_frequency_hz float

Highest observing frequency in Hz, finite and positive. This sets the shortest wavelength and hence the finest instrumental fringe scale.

required samples_per_fringe float

Number of nominal pixels per fringe, at least two. Defaults to the two-sample Nyquist estimate; larger values provide finer sampling.

2.0

Returns:

Type Description int

Smallest power-of-two nside satisfying the nominal pixel-size criterion, with a minimum of one. Values outside the supported HEALPix range (nside < 2**30) raise ValueError.

Notes

The largest angular phase gradient is \(2\pi b_{\max}/\lambda\). Using the nominal HEALPix pixel width \(\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm pix}}\) therefore gives

\[ \frac{\sqrt{\pi/3}}{N_{\rm side}} \leq \frac{c}{s\,b_{\max}\nu_{\max}}, \]

where \(s\) is samples_per_fringe. For a zero baseline there is no fringe-resolution requirement and the function returns one.

This is a baseline-based sampling estimate, not a strict spherical sampling theorem: HEALPix pixels have different shapes, and beam, sky structure and sharp horizon masks can require finer quadrature. Check visibility convergence at higher resolution when accuracy matters. The helper does not change a run's configured resolution or foreground prior. See https://healpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/generated/healpy.pixelfunc.nside2resol.html for the nominal pixel-width convention.

docs.text:
build_fourier_geometry(*, n_u: int, n_v: int, n_eta: int, du: float, dv: float, d_eta: float) -> FourierGeometry

Define the rectilinear Fourier grid of the cosmological 21-cm brightness field.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_u int

Number of transverse u modes before removing the angular monopole.

required n_v int

Number of transverse v modes before removing the angular monopole.

required n_eta int

Number of line-of-sight Fourier modes before excluding eta=0.

required du float

Transverse u spacing in inverse radians; must be positive.

required dv float

Transverse v spacing in inverse radians; must be positive.

required d_eta float

Positive eta spacing and integration weight in inverse Hz (seconds).

required

Returns:

Name Type Description geometry FourierGeometry

Retained coordinates and spacings for (n_un_v - 1)(n_eta - 1) coefficients.

Notes

The intrinsic cosmological brightness field is parameterised by complex amplitudes on a three-dimensional rectilinear (u, v, eta) grid, rather than by independent image-pixel amplitudes. The transverse coordinates u and v are Fourier duals of the reference-time image direction cosines (l, m), while eta is the Fourier dual of observing frequency. These are model coordinates, not the baselines sampled by the instrument. The transverse representation uses a local tangent-plane description of the cosmological field.

This basis provides a natural parameterisation for power-spectrum inference. At a reference redshift, the modes map to comoving wavenumbers as

\[ k_x = 2\pi u / D_M, \qquad k_y = 2\pi v / D_M, \qquad k_z = 2\pi\eta / |d\chi/d\nu|. \]

Here D_M is the transverse comoving distance and |dchi/dnu| is the line-of-sight distance per unit frequency. Under the statistically homogeneous and isotropic Gaussian signal model, distinct Fourier modes are uncorrelated and their prior variances are determined by the power spectrum at |k|. Grouping modes into spherical k bins therefore links the coefficient prior directly to the power-spectrum amplitudes inferred downstream, while the individual amplitudes can be analytically marginalised. Coordinate conversion, binning, and prior construction are separate from this geometry builder.

Every retained transverse pair is combined with every retained eta mode. The (u, v)=(0, 0) pair and eta=0 plane are excluded, leaving (n_u*n_v - 1) * (n_eta - 1) coefficients. Flattening orders v first, then u, with eta varying fastest. The spacings du, dv, and d_eta also supply the Fourier integration weights; they are normally chosen from the reciprocal transverse model extents and observing bandwidth.

Downstream, F_z maps eta modes to frequency and F' maps transverse modes to brightness at the selected HEALPix pixel centres. The primary beam and full three-dimensional fringe response then propagate this field into the measured visibilities, where instrumental coupling mixes the mode signatures. This function defines only coordinates and spacings; it does not construct a brightness realisation, prior covariance, or any of those operators.

run_multinest(setup_result: SetupResult, out_dir: Path | str, *, random_key: int | None = None, n_live_points: int | None = None, n_live_scale_factor: float = 25.0, calc_avg_eval: bool = False, avg_iters: int = 10, file_root: str = 'data-', resume: bool | None = None, verbose: bool = False, importance_nested_sampling: bool | None = None, multimodal: bool | None = None, const_efficiency_mode: bool | None = None, evidence_tolerance: float | None = None, sampling_efficiency: float | None = None, max_iter: int | None = None, print_rate: int = 100, center_likelihood: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]

Run MultiNest, or evaluate a parameter-free model analytically.

A model with no sampled hyperparameters needs no nested sampling. Its conditional MAP coefficients and marginalised log-evidence target are evaluated in one solve and saved as map_coefficients.npy and summary.json. The same fixed data/noise normalisation is omitted as in the sampled likelihood, so same-dataset model comparisons are unchanged.

This implementation is intentionally single-process at the sampler level. The expensive operation is still the likelihood evaluation itself, which can use multiple GPUs internally through the JAXMg-backed marginalized likelihood.

By default this wrapper mirrors the old BayesEoR MultiNest runner closely: aside from the required output basename and resolved live-point count, it leaves the remaining MultiNest options unset so the underlying pymultinest.solve defaults apply.

Set center_likelihood=True to subtract the log likelihood at the prior midpoint before passing values to MultiNest. This avoids loss of precision in its evidence-error estimate for bright foregrounds. The offset is restored in the returned logZ and saved in summary.json; native MultiNest files retain centred values. Resuming requires the same centring setting and uses the recorded offset unchanged.

docs.text:
Configuration for marginalized log-likelihood evaluation.

This class evaluates the analytically marginalized BayesEoR target from the compressed matrix stack

T^H N^{-1} T, T^H N^{-1} d, and d^H N^{-1} d.

Single-device inference uses a standard JAX Cholesky factorisation on CPU or GPU; multi-GPU inference uses JAXMG. Both evaluate the same Gaussian target. The large dense matrix is kept row-sharded over a 1D device mesh, while the right-hand side vector and scalar normalization term are replicated. Each likelihood call builds the diagonal prior precision Phi^{-1}, forms

Sigma = T^H N^{-1} T + Phi^{-1}

in a work matrix, and then uses one factorisation to obtain both Sigma^{-1} dbar and log|Sigma|.

Visibilities contain both each measured value and its conjugate, as produced by uvd_to_vector. They are not independent complex samples: the Gaussian exponent and log determinants therefore carry factors of one half. Foreground image coefficients are real, and cosmological Fourier coefficients obey the real-sky conjugacy constraint. A reduced operator must preserve this covariance structure, not introduce independent complex sky amplitudes.

The returned target omits fixed data/noise normalisation terms. These cancel in Bayes factors only when both models use the same dataset, noise covariance and omitted constants; see docs/inference.md.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
These functions evaluate the EoR and foreground operators as JAX arrays. They do not read files, choose hardware or apply priors, so they can be used inside compiled code. For full-size operators saved to disk, see construction.

\[ \mathbf T_{21}=\mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\mathbf F'\mathbf F_z, \qquad \mathbf T_{\rm FG}=\mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\mathbf Q_z \]

docs.title: Main interface
docs.text:
T_21 and T_fg build a block of each operator from the sky geometry, baselines and beam. T_fg_weighted applies the prior and noise weighting used by the KL reduced basis.

Linear operators used in BayesEoR's interferometric forward model.

The component models share the beam-weighted measurement operator \(R = F^{-1}P\) and differ in how their coefficients define sky brightness:

\[ m_{21} = T_{21}a, \qquad T_{21} = R F' F_z, \qquad m_{\rm FG} = T_{\rm FG}q, \qquad T_{\rm FG} = R Q_z. \]

build_transverse_fourier_operator constructs F' (uv to image), build_spectral_fourier_operator constructs F_z (eta to frequency), and build_foreground_spectral_operator supplies the spectral part of Q_z. build_sky_to_visibility_operator constructs R, including the pixel solid angle and primary beam. T_21 and T_fg compose the response and component factors for supplied blocks of visibility rows.

These functions perform numerical construction only. Geometry modules define the coordinates; construction/operator_construction.py chooses CPU blocks, distributes their construction, and saves the assembled matrices. BuildMatrices supplies the configured input arrays. The compact factors below implement these products without forming full Kronecker matrices. T_fg_weighted additionally applies supplied prior and noise factors to prepare the foreground operator for decomposition. No unit conversion or KL compression is applied.

Each factor of the operators can also be built separately: the fringe response, \(\mathbf R = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\); the Fourier transforms, \(\mathbf F'\) and \(\mathbf F_z\); and the foreground spectral basis, \(\mathbf Q_z\).

Linear operators used in BayesEoR's interferometric forward model.

The component models share the beam-weighted measurement operator \(R = F^{-1}P\) and differ in how their coefficients define sky brightness:

\[ m_{21} = T_{21}a, \qquad T_{21} = R F' F_z, \qquad m_{\rm FG} = T_{\rm FG}q, \qquad T_{\rm FG} = R Q_z. \]

build_transverse_fourier_operator constructs F' (uv to image), build_spectral_fourier_operator constructs F_z (eta to frequency), and build_foreground_spectral_operator supplies the spectral part of Q_z. build_sky_to_visibility_operator constructs R, including the pixel solid angle and primary beam. docs.title: build_sky_to_visibility_operator
docs.text:
build_sky_to_visibility_operator(lmn: Array, uvw_lambda: Array, beam: Array, pixel_area_sr: float) -> jax.Array

Map individual HEALPix pixel brightnesses to measured visibilities.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default lmn Array

Topocentric sky coordinates with shape (n_time, 3, n_pixel). Pixel identities remain fixed on the celestial sky while their topocentric direction cosines change with observing time.

required uvw_lambda Array

Baselines in observing wavelengths with shape (n_frequency, 3, n_baseline). BayesEoR follows the PyUVData ant2 - ant1 baseline convention, hence the positive phase used below is equivalent to a negative phase with the opposite ant1 - ant2 baseline convention. Baselines are fixed in the instrument frame; sky rotation is already represented by lmn.

required beam Array

Horizon-limited primary-beam power response with shape (n_time, n_frequency, n_pixel). Pixels at or below the horizon must already have zero gain.

required pixel_area_sr float

Solid angle of one equal-area sky pixel in steradians.

required

Returns:

Type Description Array

Beam-weighted sky-to-visibility response with shape (n_time, n_frequency, n_baseline, n_pixel).

Notes

At each observing time, propagate the pixels' topocentric (l, m, n) directions through the full three-dimensional discrete Fourier response, including primary-beam weighting and pixel solid angle. The combined operator is \(R=F^{-1}P\).

\[ R_{tfbp} = \Delta\Omega\,P_{tfp}\, \exp[+2\pi i\,\boldsymbol u_b(\nu_f)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)]. \]

Summing R[t, f, b, p] * brightness[f, p] over pixels gives a model visibility. Both sky components use this response, restricted to their respective pixel selections. F^{-1} denotes the sky-to-visibility Fourier operator; it does not imply a numerical matrix inversion here.

docs.text:
build_transverse_fourier_operator(uv: Array, lm: Array, uv_cell_area: float) -> jax.Array

Map cosmological (u, v) coefficients to brightness at HEALPix pixel centres.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default uv Array

Retained model coordinates, shape (2, n_uv_mode). These are the cosmological Fourier grid, not the instrument's sampled baselines.

required lm Array

Image direction cosines, shape (2, n_pixel). The caller selects the cosmological pixels at the reference time, defining a fixed transverse chart for the intrinsic brightness field.

Fourier-cell integration weight du * dv.

required

Notes

\[ F'_{pu} = \Delta u\,\Delta v\, \exp[-2\pi i(u_u l_p + v_u m_p)]. \]

docs.title: build_foreground_spectral_operator
docs.text:
build_foreground_spectral_operator(frequencies_mhz: Array, reference_frequency_mhz: float, spectral_indices: Sequence[float] = (-2.63, -2.82)) -> jax.Array

Map a pixel's foreground amplitudes to its brightness spectrum.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default frequencies_mhz Array

Observing frequencies in MHz, shape (n_frequency,).

required reference_frequency_mhz float

Positive reference frequency nu_0 in MHz. Power-law amplitudes are defined at this frequency.

required spectral_indices sequence of float

Signed exponents for the power-law components, following the constant component. For example, -2.63 gives a spectrum decreasing with frequency. BuildMatrices converts its positive beta_fg configuration values to this signed convention.

(-2.63, -2.82)

Returns:

Type Description Array

Dimensionless complex matrix of shape (n_frequency, 1 + len(spectral_indices)). It contains only the spectral factors; build_T_fg_core applies them independently to each image pixel to implement the full Q_z mapping.

Notes

These constant and power-law factors define the spectral part of \(Q_z\), shared by every foreground HEALPix pixel.

\[ Q_{f0}=1,\qquad Q_{fs}=( u_f/ u_0)^{ eta_s}\ (s>0), \qquad s_p( u_f)=\sum_s Q_{fs}q_{s,p}. \]

docs.title: build_T_21_core
docs.text:
build_T_21_core(sky_to_visibility: Array, transverse_operator: Array, spectral_operator: Array) -> jax.Array

Map cosmological (u, v, eta) amplitudes to a block of visibilities.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sky_to_visibility Array

R restricted to cosmological image pixels, with shape (n_time, n_frequency, n_baseline, n_pixel).

required transverse_operator Array

F' with shape (n_pixel, n_uv_mode). Its pixel order must match the last axis of sky_to_visibility.

required spectral_operator Array

F_z with shape (n_frequency, n_eta_mode), selected for the same frequency rows as sky_to_visibility.

required

Returns:

Type Description Array

Matrix of shape (n_time * n_frequency * n_baseline, n_uv_mode * n_eta_mode). Rows are ordered by time, frequency, then baseline; columns by transverse mode, then eta (fastest varying). Multiplication by the correspondingly ordered a gives m_21.

Notes

Reconstruct their brightness on the cosmological HEALPix selection and propagate it through the beam-weighted three-dimensional fringe response, implementing \(T_{21}=R F' F_z\).

\[ (T_{21})_{(tfb),(ue)} = \left[\sum_p R_{tfbp} F'_{pu}\right](F_z)_{fe}. \]

core denotes the equation-level calculation for supplied arrays. T_21_build_save handles distributed CPU construction and saving. All integration weights are already included in the input operators.

docs.title: build_T_fg_core
docs.text:
build_T_fg_core(sky_to_visibility: Array, spectral_operator: Array) -> jax.Array

Map spectral foreground amplitudes at each HEALPix pixel to visibilities.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sky_to_visibility Array

R for the foreground pixel selection, with shape (n_time, n_frequency, n_baseline, n_pixel).

required spectral_operator Array

Spectral factors Q from build_foreground_spectral_operator, shape (n_frequency, n_spectral_component). Frequency rows must match those in sky_to_visibility.

required

Returns:

Type Description Array

Matrix of shape (n_time * n_frequency * n_baseline, n_spectral_component * n_pixel). Rows are ordered by time, frequency, then baseline. Columns are ordered by spectral component, then pixel, matching q = (q_0.T, q_1.T, ...).T.

Notes

Evaluate each pixel's brightness at the observing frequencies and apply the beam-weighted three-dimensional fringe response, implementing \(T_{\rm FG}=R Q_z\).

\[ (T_{\rm FG})_{(tfb),(sp)} = R_{tfbp} Q_{fs}. \]

Each foreground coefficient belongs to one image pixel and one spectral component. Q supplies the spectral dependence at every pixel; R propagates the resulting brightness through the instrument.

T_fg_build_save distributes and saves blocks from this core. The pixel identity in Q_z is applied implicitly, so no dense Kronecker product or additional pixel-area factor is needed.

docs.title: weight_foreground_operator
docs.text:
weight_foreground_operator(operator: Array, prior_sqrt: Array, noise_whitener: Array) -> jax.Array

Prior-weight and noise-whiten a foreground coefficient-to-visibility matrix.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default operator Array

Physical foreground operator, shape (n_visibility, n_coefficient). Columns use spectral-component/pixel order; rows use time/frequency/baseline order, as returned by T_fg.

required prior_sqrt Array

Factor L satisfying Sigma_q = L @ L.conj().T. Supply either its diagonal as a vector of length n_coefficient (the prior standard deviations), or a square matrix for correlated coefficients. Entries have the units of the corresponding physical coefficients.

required noise_whitener Array

Factor W satisfying W @ N @ W.conj().T = I. Supply either its diagonal as a vector of length n_visibility (inverse complex noise RMS, equivalently sqrt(Ninv)), or a square whitening matrix. Noise RMS must use the units of the visibilities predicted by operator acting on the physical coefficients.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description weighted_operator Array

A = W @ operator @ L, with the same shape as operator. Maps standard-normal foreground deviations into noise-whitened visibilities.

Notes

With Hermitian covariance roots this is

\[ A = N^{-1/2} T_{\rm FG} \Sigma_q^{1/2}, \qquad A A^\dagger = W T_{\rm FG} \Sigma_q T_{\rm FG}^\dagger W^\dagger. \]

Thus an SVD of A or eigendecomposition of A @ A.conj().T can recover its noise-relevant visibility modes. This function only applies the factors: it does not construct a covariance, decompose, truncate, save, or choose a device. The caller supplies valid covariance factors; shape checks remain compatible with jax.jit and differentiation. Prior means affect the predicted mean, not this uncertainty operator.

For diagonal factors, matching row/column subsets can be weighted independently. Dense factors mix rows/columns and require the complete contracted axes; slicing their diagonal blocks generally changes the model.

docs.title: build_nudft_matrix
docs.text:
build_nudft_matrix(coords_in: ndarray, coords_out: ndarray, sign: int = -1) -> jnp.ndarray

Map amplitudes between supplied coordinate sets with a Fourier kernel.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default coords_in ndarray

Source coordinates. Shape (N_axes, N_in). e.g., Sky positions (l, m, n) for a forward transform.

required coords_out ndarray

Target coordinates. Shape (N_axes, N_out). e.g., Baselines (u, v, w) for a forward transform.

required sign int

Fourier exponent sign: -1 gives exp(-2 pi i phase) and +1 gives its complex conjugate. This is independent of the baseline convention documented in build_sky_to_visibility_operator.

-1

Returns:

Name Type Description nudft_matrix ndarray

A Complex128 matrix of shape (N_out, N_in).

Notes

For input coordinates x_i and output coordinates y_j, return

\[ K_{ji} = \exp\!\left(\mathrm{sign}\,2\pi i\,y_j\cdot x_i\right). \]

Multiplication by K maps input amplitudes to the output samples. The coordinate pairs determine the spaces being connected; sign selects the Fourier phase convention. Reversing the sign alone does not construct a matrix inverse for arbitrary non-uniform sampling. The physical operator builders supply their own integration weights.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A run is described by a RunConfig, normally read from YAML by BayesEoRParser. run_setup then loads the data, builds or reuses the operators, and returns a SetupResult holding everything the sampler needs.

from bayeseor_jax import BayesEoRParser, run_setup

config = BayesEoRParser().parse_args(["--config", "config.yaml"])
setup = run_setup(config)

See construction and execution for what setup does. Each setting is documented on the guide page it affects, and the examples show complete, commented configurations.

docs.title: bayeseor_jax.setup.run_setup
docs.text:
run_setup(config: RunConfig, *, build_foreground_kl: bool = False, kl_f: float = 0.1) -> SetupResult

Prepare the physical operators, priors and marginalised likelihood.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default config RunConfig

Requested data/model/inference settings. Actual observation axes and model coordinates are resolved locally without modifying this object.

required build_foreground_kl bool

Construct the weighted foreground operator and reduce it into config.foreground_kl_path before joint assembly. Rebuilds the basis when explicitly requested; otherwise loads the supplied basis unchanged.

False kl_f float

Maximum discarded foreground RMS relative to the noise when building the KL basis. Defaults to 0.1; ignored when loading an existing basis.

0.1

Returns:

Type Description SetupResult

Configured likelihood, coefficient and power-spectrum priors, matrix builder, selected visibility data and cosmological bin metadata.

Notes

This coordinates loading, geometry, component construction, joint assembly and likelihood products; it does not run nested sampling. KL construction uses the resolved observation, physical prior and inference noise weights. A supplied KL operator is loaded with a standard-normal prior, and is only recomputed when build_foreground_kl is explicitly enabled. Omitted image and transverse Fourier resolutions are inferred from the selected observation. Explicit values below the estimates trigger warnings but are retained; these checks do not replace convergence studies.

docs.title: Interferometric data
docs.text: BayesEoR performs cosmological inference directly on radio-interferometric visibilities, the raw measurements of an interferometer, rather than on images or power spectra estimated from them.

docs.title: Visibilities
docs.text:
An interferometer is an array of antennas whose signals are correlated in pairs. The visibility measured by antennas \(i\) and \(j\) is the time-averaged cross-correlation of their voltages,

\[ V_{ij}( u,t)=\left\langle v_i( u,t)\,v_j^{*}( u,t) ight angle. \]

Each pair forms a baseline, \( oldsymbol b_{ij}= oldsymbol r_i- oldsymbol r_j\), whose visibility measures a single Fourier mode of the beam-weighted sky. Measured in wavelengths, the baseline sets which mode is sampled,

\[ oldsymbol u_{ij}( u)= rac{ u}{c}\, oldsymbol b_{ij}. \]

Longer baselines respond to finer angular structure, and the baseline's orientation sets the direction of that structure. Because \( oldsymbol u_{ij}\) scales with frequency, the same baseline samples a different angular scale in every channel, and as the Earth rotates, the sampled modes change over the course of an observation.

docs.title: Why the instrument matters
docs.text:
Each visibility only samples the modes set by its baseline, beam, frequency and time, so the forward model is only as accurate as its description of the instrument. BayesEoR therefore needs the array layout, primary beam, observing frequencies, times and telescope location of the data being analysed:

  • Instrumental configuration: array layout and primary beam.
  • Observation configuration: frequencies, times and telescope location.
  • Visibility data: supported formats, units, ordering and noise.

docs.title: Generating realistic data
docs.text: To simulate realistic visibilities, use BayesEoR-Data-Generation. From a single YAML configuration, it builds mock-EoR, diffuse (GSM) and point-source (GLEAM-like and A-team) sky models and simulates their visibilities with pyuvsim. The resulting UVH5 files can be passed directly to BayesEoR as data_path.

docs.title: Instrumental configuration
docs.text: The instrument enters the forward model through its array layout, which sets the sampled baselines, and its primary beam, which weights the sky seen by each antenna. Both must describe the instrument that produced the data.

docs.title: Array layout
docs.text:
BayesEoR describes the array by its sampled baselines, rather than a table of antenna positions. Each baseline is a three-dimensional vector in metres, with east, north and up components in the telescope's local frame. The full vector, including the up (\(w\)) component, enters the forward model, so the wide-field geometry is preserved.

Every baseline is paired with its reversed copy, \(\boldsymbol b \to -\boldsymbol b\), which carries the conjugate visibility. The baseline axis therefore has length \(2N_{\rm bls}\): the original baselines, followed by their reversed copies in the same order.

How the baselines are supplied depends on the data format.

Visibility files (.uvh5, .uvfits, .ms)Preprocessed vectors (.npy)

The baselines are read from the file with pyuvdata, sorted by antenna pair and paired with their reversed copies automatically. The file should contain calibrated, drift-scan data, with the same baselines present at every selected time. Phased data are unprojected before use.

antenna_selection

Which antenna pairs to keep.

  • Default: cross, all cross-correlations, no autocorrelations.
  • Accepts: any string accepted by pyuvdata's UVData.select(ant_str=...), for example all or explicit pairs such as 0_1,0_2,1_2.
bl_cutoff

Removes baselines longer than the cutoff.

  • Default: none, all baselines kept.
  • Units: metres.
  • Length: the projected length \(\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\); the up component is not included.
redundant_avg

Averages groups of redundant baselines, those with the same separation and orientation, into one visibility each.

  • Default: false.
  • Redundancy: the number of baselines in each group, \(R\), is stored and reduces its noise variance in the likelihood to \(\sigma^2/R\).
uniform_redundancy

Keeps a redundancy of one for every baseline, even after averaging.

  • Default: false.
save_model

Writes the selected baselines to save_dir as uvw_model.npy, redundancy_model.npy and antpairs.npy.

  • Default: false.
  • Reuse: the files use the preprocessed format, so together with the vector written by save_vis: true they can be passed back in as a .npy input.

.npy visibility vectors carry no metadata, so point inst_model to a directory describing their baselines:

inst_model: inputs/instrument/
uvw_model.npy (required)

The baseline vectors.

  • Shape: \((N_t, 2N_{\rm bls}, 3)\), one set per integration.
  • Units: metres, not wavelengths, despite the name.
  • Components: east, north, up.
  • Order: entries \(b\) and \(N_{\rm bls}+b\) are the same baseline with opposite sign, and the order matches the data vector; see visibility ordering.
redundancy_model.npy (required)

The number of baselines averaged into each entry.

  • Shape: \((N_t, 2N_{\rm bls})\) or \((N_t, 2N_{\rm bls}, 1)\).
  • Values: ones for unaveraged data; a baseline and its reversed copy take the same value.
antpairs.npy (optional)

Antenna-pair labels, used for bookkeeping only.

  • Shape: \(2N_{\rm bls}\) tuples, in baseline order.
  • Values: for example (0, 1), with its reversed copy labelled (1, 0).

Each file can be a plain array, or a BayesEoR dictionary with the array under data, as written by save_model. A single instrument_model.npy dictionary with uvw_model, redundancy_model and optional antpairs entries can be used instead, and takes precedence if present. Dictionary files are loaded with pickle, so only load them from trusted sources.

Building the files from an array of baselines 
import numpy as np

# uvw: original baselines, shape (n_t, n_bls, 3), east/north/up in metres
uvw_model = np.concatenate([uvw, -uvw], axis=1)
redundancy_model = np.ones(uvw_model.shape[:2])

np.save("inputs/instrument/uvw_model.npy", uvw_model)
np.save("inputs/instrument/redundancy_model.npy", redundancy_model)

docs.title: Primary beam
docs.text:
The primary beam is the power response of each antenna to the sky, \(P(\hat{\boldsymbol s},\nu)\). It is evaluated along every sky pixel's track at each frequency and integration, and weights the sky before it is mapped into the visibilities. A single beam is used for all antennas, and its response is zero at and below the horizon.

Set beam_type to the name of an analytic profile, or to the path of a beam file. Below, \(\theta\) is the zenith angle.

Analytic profilesBeam files uniform

A unit response everywhere above the horizon.

  • Parameters: none.
  • Default: this is the default beam_type.
gaussian

A Gaussian in zenith angle, \(P = A\exp(-\theta^2/2\sigma^2)\).

  • Width: fwhm_deg, in degrees, for a frequency-independent width; or diam, in metres, for a chromatic width matched to the main lobe of an Airy beam.
  • Peak: peak_amp, the zenith response \(A\). Defaults to 1.
airy

The power pattern of a uniformly illuminated circular dish, \(P = [2J_1(x)/x]^2\) with \(x = \pi D\nu\sin\theta/c\).

  • Aperture: diam, the dish diameter \(D\) in metres; or fwhm_deg, from which an effective diameter is set at each frequency so that the main-lobe width is fixed.
  • Peak: always 1.
gausscosine

A Gaussian modulated by a cosine, \(P = A\exp(-\theta^2/2\sigma^2) \cos^2(\pi f_c\theta)\), adding radial structure to the beam.

  • Width: fwhm_deg or diam, as for gaussian.
  • Modulation: cosfreq, \(f_c\), in inverse radians.
  • Peak: peak_amp. Defaults to 1.
taperairy

An Airy pattern multiplied by a Gaussian taper, suppressing its sidelobes.

  • Aperture: diam, in metres.
  • Taper: fwhm_deg, the width of the Gaussian, in degrees.
  • Peak: peak_amp. Defaults to 1.
tanhairy

An Airy pattern multiplied by a smooth taper, \(1 - s\tanh(k\theta)\), that suppresses the response far from zenith.

  • Aperture: diam, in metres.
  • Rate: tanh_freq, \(k\), in inverse radians.
  • Suppression: tanh_sl_red, \(s\). Far from zenith the power is scaled by \(1-s\), so 0.99 leaves 1%.

For example:

beam_type: gaussian
fwhm_deg: 9.306821090681533

Any beamfits file readable by pyuvdata's UVBeam can be used, on either a HEALPix or an azimuth/zenith-angle grid, and as an electric-field or power beam. It is interpolated onto the sky pixels and observing frequencies, so its frequency range should cover the observation.

beam_type: inputs/beams/beam.fits
pol: pI
pol

The beam polarisation to use.

  • Default: xx.
  • Accepts: xx, yy or pI. Electric-field beams are converted to the corresponding power or pseudo-Stokes I response; power beams must already contain it.
  • Match the data: with the default form_pi: true, the data are pseudo-Stokes I, so use pol: pI.
freq_interp_kind

How the beam is interpolated between its tabulated frequencies.

  • Default: cubic.
  • Accepts: any SciPy interp1d kind, such as linear or cubic.

Tip

Beam sidelobes matter. If the beam has a non-negligible response outside the EoR field of view, set the foreground field of view, fov_fg, larger than fov_eor. See the foreground model.

docs.title: Observation configuration
docs.text:
The observation sets when and where the sky was observed: the frequency channels, the integration times and the telescope location. Together these fix where each sky direction lies relative to the instrument and the horizon at every integration.

For visibility files, the frequencies and times are read from the file and can be down-selected. Preprocessed .npy vectors carry no metadata, so their axes are defined in the configuration instead. The telescope location is always set in the configuration.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
Visibility files (.uvh5, .uvfits, .ms)Preprocessed vectors (.npy)

All channels in the file are used unless a starting option is set. Choose one starting option and, optionally, a width:

freq_idx_min

Starts at a channel index.

  • Units: zero-based channel index.
freq_min

Starts at the first channel at or above this frequency.

  • Units: Hz.
freq_center

Selects a window centred on the channel nearest this frequency.

  • Units: Hz.
  • Requires: n_freqs_select.
n_freqs_select

The number of channels to keep.

  • Default: all channels from the starting channel onwards.
  • Note: has no effect without a starting option.

If more than one starting option is set, freq_center takes precedence, then freq_min. The parser still requires n_freq, f0_mhz and df_mhz, but their values are replaced by the selected channels.

The channels are defined directly, as \( u_f = u_0 + f\,\Delta u\) for \(f = 0, \dots, N_ u - 1\):

n_freq: 38
f0_mhz: 158.304048743
df_mhz: 0.23761898685801028
n_freq The number of channels, \(N_ u\). f0_mhz

The frequency of the first channel, \( u_0\).

  • Units: MHz.
df_mhz

The channel spacing, \(\Delta u\).

  • Units: MHz.

docs.text:
Visibility files (.uvh5, .uvfits, .ms)Preprocessed vectors (.npy)

All integrations in the file are used unless a starting option is set. Choose one starting option and, optionally, a width:

jd_idx_min

Starts at an integration index.

  • Units: zero-based index.
jd_min

Starts at the first integration at or after this time.

  • Units: Julian date.
jd_center

Selects a window centred on the integration nearest this time.

  • Units: Julian date.
  • Requires: n_times_select.
n_times_select

The number of integrations to keep.

  • Default: all integrations from the starting one onwards.
  • Note: has no effect without a starting option.

If more than one starting option is set, jd_center takes precedence, then jd_min. The integration time is read from the file.

The integrations are defined directly, as \(N_t\) evenly spaced times:

n_t: 1
d_t: 10.0
jd_center: 2461040.5
n_t

The number of integrations, \(N_t\).

  • Default: 1.
  • Note: must match the time axis of the instrument model.
d_t

The spacing between integrations.

  • Units: seconds.
  • Note: required, even for a single integration.
jd_min or jd_center

Anchors the times. One is required.

  • Units: Julian date.
  • jd_min: the first integration.
  • jd_center: the integration at index \(\lfloor N_t/2 \rfloor\).
  • Precedence: jd_min, if both are set.

docs.text:
telescope_latlonalt: [-30.72152777777791, 21.428305555555557, 1073.0000000093132]
telescope_latlonalt

The telescope's geodetic position, as [latitude, longitude, altitude].

docs.title: Visibility data
docs.text: Set data_path to the visibilities to analyse. The loader reads them, converts them to the analysis units and arranges them in the same order as the rows of the forward model. It does not calibrate the data or simulate a sky, and the instrumental and observation settings must describe the same data.

docs.title: Input formats
docs.text:
The reader is chosen from the file suffix. Simulated and observed visibilities are handled in the same way.

Visibility files (.uvh5, .uvfits, .ms)Preprocessed vectors (.npy) 
data_path: inputs/observation.uvh5

Files are read with pyuvdata, so .ms Measurement Sets need pyuvdata's optional casacore dependency. The data should be:

  • Calibrated, in Jy or K sr. They are converted to mK sr, using the Rayleigh–Jeans relation for each channel.
  • Drift-scan, with the same baselines at every selected time. Phased data are unprojected before use.
  • Flagged with care. Fully flagged baselines are removed, but partial flags are not turned into per-visibility weights, so check flagging before inference.

BayesEoR's sky model is scalar, so the data are reduced to one polarisation:

form_pi

Forms pseudo-Stokes I visibilities.

  • Default: true.
  • Requires: XX and YY in the file, or an existing pI polarisation, which is kept as it is.
pi_norm

The normalisation in \(\mathrm{pI} = N(\mathrm{XX} + \mathrm{YY})\).

  • Default: 1, not one half.
pol

The polarisation to keep when form_pi: false.

  • Default: xx.
  • Note: the same setting selects the polarisation of a beam file.
save_vis

Writes the prepared vector to save_dir as vis_vector.npy, plus noise_vector.npy if calc_noise is set.

  • Default: false.
  • Reuse: with save_model: true, the outputs can be passed back in as a .npy input.

A .npy file holds the complex data vector itself, already in mK sr and in the data vector ordering below. It can be a plain array, or a BayesEoR dictionary with the vector under data. Dictionary files are loaded with pickle, so only load them from trusted sources.

The file carries no metadata, so the instrument model and observation axes must be given in full:

data_path: inputs/visibilities.npy
inst_model: inputs/instrument/
n_freq: 38
f0_mhz: 158.304048743
df_mhz: 0.23761898685801028
n_t: 1
d_t: 10.0
jd_center: 2461040.5

See array layout for inst_model, and observation configuration for the axes. Metadata stored inside a dictionary file are not used.

docs.title: Data vector ordering
docs.text:
The data are a single complex vector with time varying slowest, then frequency, then baseline. Within each time and frequency, the \(N_{\rm bls}\) original baselines are followed by their reversed copies, which hold the conjugate visibilities:

\[ \boldsymbol d_{tf} =\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol v_{tf}\\\boldsymbol v_{tf}^{*}\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{row} = (t\,N_\nu + f)\,2N_{\rm bls} + b. \]

The vector therefore has length \(2N_tN_\nu N_{\rm bls}\). The conjugate copies are not independent measurements; the marginalised likelihood accounts for this. Visibility files are arranged this way automatically, but a .npy vector, its noise vectors and the instrument model must already follow it.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
The loader decides whether the data already contain noise. The first option that applies is used:

noise_data_path

A noise vector for data that already contain noise.

  • Effect: the data are used unchanged.
  • Format: a .npy vector in mK sr, in the data vector ordering.
calc_noise

Estimates the noise of a visibility file from differences between even and odd integrations.

  • Default: false.
  • Effect: the data are used unchanged.
  • Requires: a visibility file with more than one integration; it has no effect on .npy inputs.
sigma and noise_seed

If neither of the above is set, the data are treated as noiseless and a Gaussian noise realisation is added.

  • sigma: the complex noise RMS per visibility before redundancy averaging, in mK sr. Each baseline's noise is scaled by \(1/\sqrt{R}\), and the reversed copies receive the conjugate noise.
  • noise_seed: the random seed. Defaults to 742123.
  • Note: sigma: 0 adds no noise.

Warning

Without noise_data_path or calc_noise, noise is added. Do not leave them unset for measurements that already contain noise.

This only determines the data. The noise covariance that weights the likelihood is set separately; see noise covariance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The examples take BayesEoR through its full workflow, from noiseless simulated visibilities to a recovered 21-cm power spectrum. Both use the same HERA-like observation, a reduced version of the one analysed in Tutt et al. (2026), and each runs on a laptop CPU in a few minutes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• 21-cm only: infer the power spectrum of a cosmological signal on its own.
  • 21-cm and foregrounds: add bright foregrounds, compress them into a KL reduced basis and infer the power spectrum jointly.

Each example has its own data, configuration and entry point in the repository's examples/ folder, and runs from the repository root after installation:

python -m examples.eor.run --sample
python -m examples.eor_fgs.run --sample

Without --sample, each stops after setup, having loaded the data, added noise and built the operators.

docs.title: 21-cm and foregrounds
docs.text:
This example adds diffuse Galactic emission and bright point sources to the same 21-cm signal and observation. The foregrounds are compressed into a KL reduced basis during setup and inferred jointly with the signal, so their uncertainty is carried into the recovered power spectrum.

DataRunningResults

The observation is identical to the 21-cm only example, with the same array, beam, band, integrations, noise and 21-cm realisation. Two foreground components are added within the same 10° field:

Diffuse emission The Global Sky Model (GSM2008), at HEALPix Nside=128. Point sources A statistical population of extragalactic sources, together with the catalogued bright A-team sources, each at its individual position.

All three components were propagated through the beam and full three-dimensional fringe response, and summed into a single noiseless data vector. simulation.json records the seeds and provenance of each component.

examples/eor_fgs/
├── config.yaml
├── run.py
└── data/
    ├── visibilities.npy             # noiseless 21-cm + foreground data, in mK sr
    ├── uvw_model.npy                # baseline vectors
    ├── redundancy_model.npy         # baseline redundancies
    ├── injected_power_spectrum.npy  # the injected P(k)
    └── simulation.json              # full simulation record

python -m examples.eor_fgs.run --sample runs every step below; without --sample, it stops after setup, including the KL construction.

1. Configure the run. config.yaml extends the 21-cm only configuration with the foreground model and the path of its reduced basis:

# Model and data
model: eor+fg                       # fit the 21-cm signal and foregrounds jointly
# Noiseless data vector
data_path: examples/eor_fgs/data/visibilities.npy
inst_model: examples/eor_fgs/data   # baselines and redundancies
# Saved operators
array_save_directory: outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128/matrices
# Sampler outputs and metadata
output_dir: outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128
# KL basis, built in setup
foreground_kl_path: outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128/kl/T_fg_reduced.npy

# Observation
n_freq: 15                          # number of channels
f0_mhz: 158.3984375                 # first channel, MHz
df_mhz: 0.09765625                  # channel spacing, MHz
n_t: 15                             # number of integrations
d_t: 21.511369943618774             # integration spacing, s
jd_center: 2459999.097166265        # central integration, JD
# HERA site
telescope_latlonalt: [-30.72152777777791, 21.428305555555557, 1073.0000000093132]

# Instrument
beam_type: airy                     # Airy primary beam
diam: 14.2                          # dish diameter, m

# Sky models
fov_eor: 10.0                       # EoR field diameter, degrees
fov_fg: 10.0                        # foreground field diameter, degrees
beta_fg: [2.63, 2.82]               # foreground power-law indices
nside: 128                          # HEALPix resolution of both models
footprint_nside: 64                 # grid on which the field boundary is chosen

# Noise
sigma: 0.006464                     # complex noise RMS, mK sr
noise_seed: 742123                  # seed for the added noise

# Inference
# Prior range on log10(Δ²/mK²), one pair per bin
priors: [[-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6]]
n_live_scale_factor: 10             # live points = 10 × parameters
random_key: 42                      # sampler seed

The foreground prior widths use their defaults; see foreground_prior_std_mk.

2. Build the model and reduced basis. Setup builds the prior- and noise-weighted foreground operator, compresses it and assembles the joint model, in a single call:

from bayeseor_jax import BayesEoRParser, run_setup

config = BayesEoRParser().parse_args(
    ["--config", "examples/eor_fgs/config.yaml", "--run"]
)
setup = run_setup(config, build_foreground_kl=True)

The physical foreground model has 1,248 coefficients: three spectral amplitudes in each of 416 pixels. Truncating at \(f = 0.1\) retains 179 KL modes, with the discarded foreground RMS at 9.5% of the noise RMS, in about 2 s on a laptop CPU. With the 1,680 EoR coefficients, the likelihood marginalises 1,859 coefficients and samples the same six power-spectrum amplitudes. Without build_foreground_kl=True, setup loads an existing basis from foreground_kl_path.

3. Sample the power spectrum. Sampling is the same as in the 21-cm only example:

from bayeseor_jax import run_nestedsampling

summary = run_nestedsampling(
    setup,
    out_dir="outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128/nested_sampling",
    random_key=config.random_key,
    n_live_scale_factor=config.n_live_scale_factor,
    center_likelihood=True,
)

Outputs are written under outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128/, with the KL basis, its singular values and truncation diagnostics under kl/.

4. Summarise the posterior. save_analysis writes the figure in Results to examples/eor_fgs/plots/:

from bayeseor_jax.analyze import save_analysis

save_analysis(
    "outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128/nested_sampling",
    output_dir="examples/eor_fgs/plots",
    metadata_dir="outputs/laptop_eor_fgs_nside128",
    label="Cosmological signal + foregrounds",
    uplim_inds=[True, False, False, False, False, False],
)

With foregrounds included, the five highest-\(k\) bins are recovered as precisely as in the 21-cm only example. The lowest bin, \(k = 0.26\ \mathrm{Mpc^{-1}}\), is no longer bounded from below: its posterior extends to the edge of the prior, since these large, spectrally smooth scales are where the signal is most degenerate with the foregrounds. The injected value still lies within its 95% interval, so the foreground uncertainty is propagated into the power spectrum rather than biasing it.

The lowest-\(k\) bin is shown as a 95% upper limit in the power-spectrum panel; the other bins show central 68% credible intervals. The right-hand panels display the full marginal posteriors.

docs.title: 21-cm only
docs.text:
With no foregrounds in the data, this example isolates the EoR model: a simulated 21-cm signal, observed by a compact HERA-like array, is recovered as a power spectrum and compared directly with the spectrum that was injected.

DataRunningResults

The observation is a short drift scan by a compact hexagonal array, of the kind used by HERA. A simulated 21-cm signal is observed for a few minutes over a narrow band, and thermal noise is added during setup.

Array 37 antennas on a 14.6 m hexagonal grid, keeping the 15 independent baselines shorter than 40 m (30 with their reversed copies). Primary beam An Airy pattern for a 14.2 m dish. Band 15 channels from 158.40 to 159.77 MHz, spaced by 97.66 kHz. Integrations 15, spaced by 21.5 s, centred on JD 2459999.097. Sky A Gaussian random field with independent 6.4 mK pixels at HEALPix Nside=256, within a 10° field. This has a flat dimensional power spectrum, \(P(k) \approx 8.84\times10^4\ \mathrm{mK^2\,Mpc^3}\), which is the injected spectrum to recover. Noise Complex Gaussian noise with RMS 0.006464 mK sr, added with a fixed seed.

The data are 6,750 complex visibilities, or 3,375 independent measurements once the conjugate copies are accounted for. They are supplied as a noiseless .npy vector with its instrument model, so no sky simulation is needed to run the example.

examples/eor/
├── config.yaml
├── run.py
└── data/
    ├── visibilities.npy             # noiseless data vector, in mK sr
    ├── uvw_model.npy                # baseline vectors
    ├── redundancy_model.npy         # baseline redundancies
    ├── injected_power_spectrum.npy  # the injected P(k)
    └── simulation.json              # full simulation record

python -m examples.eor.run --sample runs every step below; without --sample, it stops after setup.

1. Configure the run. config.yaml describes the data, the observation and the model:

# Model and data
model: eor                          # fit the 21-cm signal only
# Noiseless data vector
data_path: examples/eor/data/visibilities.npy
inst_model: examples/eor/data       # baselines and redundancies
# Saved operators
array_save_directory: outputs/laptop_eor_nside128/matrices
# Sampler outputs and metadata
output_dir: outputs/laptop_eor_nside128

# Observation
n_freq: 15                          # number of channels
f0_mhz: 158.3984375                 # first channel, MHz
df_mhz: 0.09765625                  # channel spacing, MHz
n_t: 15                             # number of integrations
d_t: 21.511369943618774             # integration spacing, s
jd_center: 2459999.097166265        # central integration, JD
# HERA site
telescope_latlonalt: [-30.72152777777791, 21.428305555555557, 1073.0000000093132]

# Instrument
beam_type: airy                     # Airy primary beam
diam: 14.2                          # dish diameter, m

# EoR model
fov_eor: 10.0                       # model field diameter, degrees
nside: 128                          # HEALPix resolution of the model
footprint_nside: 64                 # grid on which the field boundary is chosen

# Noise
sigma: 0.006464                     # complex noise RMS, mK sr
noise_seed: 742123                  # seed for the added noise

# Inference
# Prior range on log10(Δ²/mK²), one pair per bin
priors: [[-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6], [-1, 6]]
n_live_scale_factor: 10             # live points = 10 × parameters
random_key: 42                      # sampler seed

See the Data, Model and Inference pages for each setting.

2. Build the model. run_setup loads the data, adds the noise, and builds the EoR operator and likelihood products:

from bayeseor_jax import BayesEoRParser, run_setup

config = BayesEoRParser().parse_args(
    ["--config", "examples/eor/config.yaml", "--run"]
)
setup = run_setup(config)

The Fourier grid is sized automatically to \(11 \times 11\) transverse and 14 line-of-sight modes, giving 1,680 EoR coefficients in six power-spectrum bins. The coefficients are marginalised analytically, so only the six bin amplitudes are sampled.

3. Sample the power spectrum. run_nestedsampling explores the posterior on the six amplitudes with MultiNest, and evaluates the evidence:

from bayeseor_jax import run_nestedsampling

summary = run_nestedsampling(
    setup,
    out_dir="outputs/laptop_eor_nside128/nested_sampling",
    random_key=config.random_key,
    n_live_scale_factor=config.n_live_scale_factor,
    center_likelihood=True,   # numerical offset, restored in the evidence
)

The noisy data, saved operators, chains and summary.json are written under outputs/laptop_eor_nside128/.

4. Summarise the posterior. save_analysis reads the chains, summarises each bin and writes the figure in Results to examples/eor/plots/:

from bayeseor_jax.analyze import save_analysis

save_analysis(
    "outputs/laptop_eor_nside128/nested_sampling",
    output_dir="examples/eor/plots",
    metadata_dir="outputs/laptop_eor_nside128",
    label="Cosmological signal only",
)

All six power-spectrum amplitudes are recovered, with the injected spectrum (dashed) inside the 95% credible interval of every bin. The posteriors are compact and well separated from the prior edges, showing that the data constrain each scale.
