docs.title: Inference
docs.text: BayesEoR accelerates joint posterior inference and Bayesian-evidence evaluation by analytically marginalising over the individual sky coefficients, and sampling only the power spectrum of the 21-cm field. These few power-spectrum amplitudes define the prior on the coefficients in each \(k\) bin, so the sampler explores tens of parameters rather than tens of thousands.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Δ² parameterisation: how the EoR coefficients are grouped into \(k\) bins, whose power-spectrum amplitudes set their prior and are the parameters sampled.
  • Analytical marginalisation: integrating out the coefficients to give a likelihood for the power spectrum alone.
  • Maximum a posteriori: recovering the coefficients and model visibilities for a fixed prior, and the foreground-only evidence.
  • Running inference: choosing the model and exploring the posterior and evidence with nested sampling.
  • Posterior analysis: reading, summarising and plotting the results.

docs.title: Maximum a posteriori
docs.text: Marginalisation does not discard the sky coefficients. For a fixed prior, either at a chosen power spectrum or for the fixed foreground prior alone, their posterior is Gaussian, and its mean, which is also its maximum, follows from the same linear system used by the marginalised likelihood.

docs.title: Conditional coefficients and visibilities
docs.text:
At a given power spectrum, the solve that evaluates the likelihood also gives the maximum a posteriori (MAP) coefficients, and hence the model visibilities of each component.

MathsCode \[ \widehat{\boldsymbol b}(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\mathbf\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\varphi)\,\overline{\boldsymbol d}, \qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol m}(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\mathbf T\,\widehat{\boldsymbol b}(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\mathbf T_{21}\widehat{\boldsymbol a} +\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\widehat{\boldsymbol q}'. \]

The conditional posterior covariance of the coefficients is \(\mathbf\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\varphi)\).

MaximumAPosteriori reuses the likelihood products from setup:

import numpy as np
from bayeseor_jax import MaximumAPosteriori

likelihood = setup.likelihood_class
map_solver = MaximumAPosteriori(
    t_ninv_t=likelihood.t_ninv_t, dbar=likelihood.dbar,
    d_ninv_d=likelihood.d_ninv_d, n_data=likelihood.n_data,
    phi_inv_class=setup.phi_inverse_class, k_vals=setup.k_vals,
    n_power_params=likelihood.n_power_params,
)
b_hat, log_post = map_solver.map_estimate(dmps=dmps)   # Δ² in mK², per bin

T = np.load("matrices/T.npy", mmap_mode="r")
m_hat = T @ np.asarray(b_hat)

The first \(N_{21}\) entries of b_hat are the EoR coefficients, and the rest the foreground coefficients.

These reconstructions are useful for inspecting residuals, \(\boldsymbol d - \widehat{\boldsymbol m}\), and the separate component models. They are conditional on the chosen power spectrum, and do not replace the marginalised power-spectrum posterior.

docs.title: Foreground-only evidence
docs.text:
A foreground-only model has no sampled parameters: its prior is fixed, so the marginalised likelihood is itself the Bayesian evidence, and is evaluated in a single solve.

MathsCode \[ \mathcal Z_{\rm FG} =\int\mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol q')\, \pi(\boldsymbol q')\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol q', \qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol q}' =\mathbf\Sigma_{\rm FG}^{-1}\,\overline{\boldsymbol d}_{\rm FG}, \]

with \(\mathbf\Sigma_{\rm FG}\) and \(\overline{\boldsymbol d}_{\rm FG}\) formed from \(\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\) alone. This evidence is the null hypothesis against which the joint model is compared.

With model: fg, running inference skips sampling and writes:

  • summary.json: the evidence, with sampler: analytic and logZerr: 0.
  • map_coefficients.npy: the MAP foreground coefficients, \(\widehat{\boldsymbol q}'\).

docs.title: Analytical marginalisation
docs.text: The forward model is linear in the sky coefficients, and both their prior and the noise are Gaussian, so the coefficients can be integrated out exactly. This leaves a likelihood for the power spectrum alone, in which the uncertainty in every coefficient, and the degeneracies between the EoR and foregrounds, are fully propagated.

docs.title: 1. Combine the components
docs.text:
The EoR and foreground contributions combine into a single linear model over the joint coefficient vector, \(\boldsymbol b\), with a block-diagonal Gaussian prior.

MathsCode \[ \boldsymbol m =\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf T_{21}&\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf T} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol a\\\boldsymbol q'\end{pmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol b}, \qquad \mathbf\Psi(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf\Phi(\boldsymbol\varphi)&\mathbf 0\\ \mathbf 0&\mathbf\Sigma'_{\rm FG} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\(\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\) is either the physical foreground operator, with prior \(\mathbf\Sigma'_{\rm FG}=\mathbf\Sigma_q\), or its reduced basis, with \(\mathbf\Sigma'_{\rm FG}=\mathbf I\). Only the EoR block, \(\mathbf\Phi\), depends on the power spectrum; the foreground prior is fixed.

Setup assembles \(\mathbf T\) as T.npy, and the diagonal of \(\mathbf\Psi^{-1}(\boldsymbol\varphi)\) is returned by PhiInverse. The foreground widths are foreground_prior_std_mk for the physical basis, or ones for a reduced basis.

docs.title: 2. The prior-predictive covariance
docs.text:
Integrating over \(\boldsymbol b\) leaves a Gaussian likelihood for the data, whose covariance combines the noise with the uncertainty each component induces in the visibilities.

MathsCode \[ \mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol\varphi) =\int\mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol b)\, \pi(\boldsymbol b\mid\boldsymbol\varphi)\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol b =\mathcal{CN}\big(\boldsymbol d;\,\boldsymbol 0,\,\mathbf C(\boldsymbol\varphi)\big), \] \[ \mathbf C(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\mathbf N +\underbrace{\mathbf T_{21}\mathbf\Phi(\boldsymbol\varphi)\mathbf T_{21}^\dagger}_{\text{EoR}} +\underbrace{\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\mathbf\Sigma'_{\rm FG}\mathbf T_{\rm FG}'^\dagger}_{\text{foregrounds, fixed}}. \]

The foreground term is the same for every proposed power spectrum. Its structure is what the KL reduced basis compresses.

The \(N_{\rm d}\times N_{\rm d}\) covariance is never built. The equivalent coefficient-space form below is used instead.

docs.title: 3. Evaluate in coefficient space
docs.text:
The same likelihood can be written in terms of a system the size of the coefficient vector. Its fixed parts are computed once during setup, so each proposed power spectrum needs only one Cholesky factorisation.

MathsCode

With the fixed products

\[ \mathbf G=\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\mathbf T, \qquad \overline{\boldsymbol d}=\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\boldsymbol d, \qquad Q=\boldsymbol d^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\boldsymbol d, \]

each proposal forms and solves

\[ \mathbf\Sigma(\boldsymbol\varphi) =\mathbf G+\mathbf\Psi^{-1}(\boldsymbol\varphi), \qquad \mathbf\Sigma(\boldsymbol\varphi)\,\widehat{\boldsymbol b} =\overline{\boldsymbol d}, \]

giving the log likelihood

\[ \ln\mathcal L =-\frac12\left[ \ln\det\mathbf\Sigma+\ln\det\mathbf\Psi -\overline{\boldsymbol d}^{\dagger}\widehat{\boldsymbol b}\right] +c_{\rm fixed}, \qquad c_{\rm fixed}=-\frac12\left[Q+\ln\det\mathbf N+N_{\rm d}\ln\pi\right]. \]

The factors of one half arise because \(\boldsymbol d\) holds each visibility and its conjugate, so it contains only \(N_{\rm d}/2\) independent measurements (see data vector ordering). The single Cholesky factorisation of \(\mathbf\Sigma\) supplies both the solve and the determinant, and is the dominant cost of each evaluation.

MarginalisedLikelihood evaluates this for a vector of log amplitudes, omitting \(c_{\rm fixed}\):

likelihood = setup.likelihood_class
log_l = likelihood.log_likelihood(rho)

On one CPU or GPU it uses a native JAX Cholesky factorisation; across several GPUs it uses JAXMg.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The likelihood is set by the two fixed covariances that are not sampled: the noise, \(\mathbf N\), and the foreground prior, \(\mathbf\Sigma_q\).

docs.title: Noise covariance
docs.text:
The likelihood assumes Gaussian thermal noise with a diagonal covariance, \(\mathbf N\), whose entries are the variance \(\langle|n|^2\rangle\) of each complex visibility. It is set by one of:

sigma

The default model, with variance \(N_{tfb} = \sigma^2/R_{tb}\) for a baseline of redundancy \(R_{tb}\) (see array layout).

  • Units: mK sr, the complex RMS per visibility before redundancy averaging.
  • Required: unless effective_noise_path is set, including when the data use noise_data_path or calc_noise.
effective_noise_path

Per-visibility noise amplitudes, replacing the sigma model.

  • Format: a .npy vector of length \(2N_tN_\nu N_{\rm bls}\), in the data vector ordering; its squared magnitudes are the variances.
  • Note: it only changes the weights. It does not affect whether noise is added to the data.

A noise vector supplied with noise_data_path, or estimated with calc_noise, does not set these weights, so sigma should still describe the noise level of the data. See noise in the data.

docs.title: Foreground prior
docs.text:
foreground_prior_std_mk

The prior standard deviation of each foreground spectral component.

  • Default: [8690.96, 2479547.30, 1406322.41].
  • Units: mK.
  • Format: one value for the constant term and one per entry of beta_fg; each is applied to every pixel.
  • Note: not used with foreground_kl_path, whose coefficients have a unit prior.

docs.title: Posterior analysis
docs.text: After sampling, the weighted MultiNest chains give the posterior on \(\Delta^2_{21}(k)\) in each bin. DataContainer reads them together with the setup metadata and summarises each bin, while the plotting helpers produce the standard power-spectrum and posterior figures.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
Setup and sampling write the following to the run's output directories.

summary.json The sampler settings, dimensions, output paths and evidence, logZ and logZerr. data-*.txt The standard MultiNest products. The weighted chain is usually data-.txt; a shorter file root may be used to stay within MultiNest's path-length limit. args.json The full run configuration, used for prior ranges when plotting. k-vals.txt, k-vals-bins.txt, k-vals-nsamples.txt

The representative \(k\), edges and number of modes of each power-spectrum bin.

  • Note: only written when the model includes the EoR.
map_coefficients.npy The MAP foreground coefficients, written instead of a chain for model: fg.

docs.title: Saving the standard analysis
docs.text:
The example pipeline calls save_analysis automatically after sampling. It uses the same weighted statistics and plotting functions described below, writing a JSON summary and a single titled PNG combining the power spectrum and marginal posteriors.

Colours default to blue for 21-cm-only models and red for joint 21-cm + foreground models, using the saved model configuration. Pass uplim_inds to save_analysis to display selected bins as 95% upper limits instead of central credible intervals.

from bayeseor_jax.analyze import save_analysis

save_analysis(
    "outputs/run_a/nested_sampling",
    metadata_dir="outputs/run_a",
    output_dir="outputs/run_a/plots",
    label="Cosmological signal + foregrounds",
)

This can also regenerate figures from completed runs without resampling. Existing analysis files are replaced; the chains remain unchanged.

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
CodeAttributes 
from bayeseor_jax import DataContainer

dc = DataContainer(
    ["outputs/run_a/multinest", "outputs/run_b/multinest"],
    labels=["Run A", "Run B"],
)
dc.medians[0]          # posterior median of each bin, in mK²
dc.cred_intervals[0]   # {68: {"lo": ..., "hi": ...}, 95: {...}}
dc.uplims[0]           # 95% upper limits, in mK²
samples, weights The sampled \(\log_{10}\) powers and their normalised posterior weights. avgs, medians, uplims Weighted means, medians and upper limits of \(\Delta^2_{21}(k)\), in mK². cred_intervals Central credible intervals, by percentage, then lo or hi. k_vals, k_vals_bins The representative \(k\) and bin edges, in Mpc⁻¹. summaries, args Each run's summary.json, including its evidence, and args.json.

Each is a list with one entry per run.

DataContainer takes the following options:

labels

One label per run, used in the plots.

  • Default: the directory names.
metadata_dirs

A setup directory holding k-vals*.txt and args.json, if these are not beside the chains.

  • Format: one directory shared by every run, or one per run.
cred_intervals, uplim_quantile

The central intervals and the upper-limit quantile.

  • Default: 68 and 95 per cent; 0.95.
expected_dmps or expected_ps A reference spectrum to plot against, as \(\Delta^2(k)\) in mK² or \(P(k)\) in mK² Mpc³. bins_correspond

Allows posterior overlays between runs whose bins describe the same shells but have slightly different mean \(k\), for example after changing the Fourier grid.

  • Default: false.
  • Note: only set this after checking the bins correspond; it does not rebin the samples.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
The plotting helpers take a DataContainer and return Matplotlib figures and axes, styled for publication without changing global Matplotlib settings.

from bayeseor_jax.analyze import (
    plot_power_spectra, plot_posteriors, plot_power_spectra_and_posteriors,
)

fig, ax = plot_power_spectra(dc, plot_priors=True)
fig, axes = plot_posteriors(dc, plot_priors=True)
fig, (power_ax, posterior_axes) = plot_power_spectra_and_posteriors(dc)
fig.savefig("power_spectrum.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plot_priors

Shades the prior range of each bin.

  • Requires: args.json, and k-vals-bins.txt for the spectrum panel.
cred_interval

The credible interval shown on the power spectrum.

  • Default: 68.
uplim_inds

Bins to show as upper limits rather than constraints.

  • Format: one boolean mask shared by every run, or one per run.
  • Note: bins are not classified automatically.
normalisation

How the posterior curves are scaled.

  • Default: peak, normalising each curve to a peak of one for comparing shapes.
  • Alternative: density, for a unit-integral density per dex.

docs.title: Reporting results
docs.text:
For each bin, report its representative \(k\), the posterior median, the credible interval used, and whether it is a constraint or an upper limit, with the quantile stated. To make a result reproducible, archive:

  • the configuration file and args.json;
  • summary.json, the chains and the k-vals*.txt files;
  • the Git commit and the JAX, JAXMg and CUDA versions;
  • the configuration needed to rebuild the saved arrays.

docs.title: Δ² parameterisation
docs.text: A detection of the 21-cm signal concerns the power on each spatial scale, not a particular realisation of the field. BayesEoR therefore treats the EoR coefficients as a statistically homogeneous and isotropic Gaussian field, whose variance is set by the dimensionless power spectrum, \(\Delta^2_{21}(k)\), in a set of spherical \(k\) bins. These bin amplitudes are the hyperparameters of the model, and the only parameters explored by the sampler.

docs.title: 1. Convert the Fourier modes to wavenumbers
docs.text:
Each EoR coefficient belongs to a mode \((u, v, \eta)\), which corresponds to a comoving wavenumber at the central redshift of the observation.

MathsCode \[ k_x=\frac{2\pi u}{D_{\rm M}(z_{\rm c})},\qquad k_y=\frac{2\pi v}{D_{\rm M}(z_{\rm c})},\qquad k_z=\frac{2\pi\eta}{|\mathrm d\chi/\mathrm d\nu|}, \]

where \(D_{\rm M}\) is the transverse comoving distance and \(\mathrm d\chi/\mathrm d\nu\) the comoving distance per unit frequency. Each mode has magnitude \(k=(k_x^2+k_y^2+k_z^2)^{1/2}\).

generate_k_modes_in_physical_coordinates returns the wavenumber magnitude of each mode, in the same order as the columns of \(\mathbf T_{21}\). This continues the example on the EoR model page.

from bayeseor_jax.model.cosmology.transforms import Cosmology
from bayeseor_jax.model.cosmology.power_spectrum import (
    generate_k_modes_in_physical_coordinates,
)

cosmology = Cosmology()
redshift = cosmology.f2z(jnp.mean(frequencies_hz))
k = generate_k_modes_in_physical_coordinates(
    grid.uv, grid.eta,
    float(cosmology.dL_dth(redshift)),
    float(jnp.abs(cosmology.dL_df(redshift))),
)
assert k.shape == (T.shape[1],)

docs.title: 2. Group the modes into spherical bins
docs.text:
Modes with similar \(|k|\) are grouped into spherical shells, each with a single power-spectrum amplitude. Only shells containing at least one mode are kept, and these define the sampled parameters.

MathsCode

The shell edges are geometric. With \(\Delta k_\parallel = 2\pi/L_\parallel\) for a line-of-sight box length \(L_\parallel\), the upper edges are

\[ k^{\rm high}_s = 2\,\Delta k_\parallel\,g^{\,s},\qquad g = 1.35, \]

and mode \(i\) belongs to bin \(s(i)\) if \(k^{\rm high}_{s-1} < k_i \leq k^{\rm high}_s\). Each bin is represented by the mean \(k_s\) of its modes, and assigned the amplitude

\[ \varphi_s \equiv \Delta^2_{21}(k_s)=\frac{k_s^3}{2\pi^2}P_{21}(k_s). \]

generate_k_cube_model_spherical_binning assigns each mode to a bin. Setup does this automatically and writes the result to the output directory:

  • k-vals.txt: the representative \(k_s\) of each bin.
  • k-vals-bins.txt: the bin edges.
  • k-vals-nsamples.txt: the number of modes in each bin.

docs.title: 3. Set the coefficient prior
docs.text:
Taking distinct Fourier modes to be uncorrelated, the prior on the EoR coefficients is diagonal, with each variance set by the amplitude of its bin.

MathsCode \[ \langle a_i a_j^*\rangle =\left[\mathbf\Phi(\boldsymbol\varphi)\right]_{ij} \propto \varphi_{s(i)}\,\delta_{ij}. \]

The constant of proportionality is the Fourier-volume normalisation, which converts \(\Delta^2_{21}(k_s)\) into the variance of a single coefficient. Each amplitude is sampled through

\[ \rho_s = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\varphi_s}{\mathrm{mK}^2}\right), \]

with an independent uniform prior on each \(\rho_s\).

PhiInverse applies the normalisation and returns the diagonal prior precision of the joint coefficients for a given set of amplitudes. Its foreground block is fixed; see analytical marginalisation.

from bayeseor_jax import run_setup

setup = run_setup(config)
# rho: one log10 amplitude per bin
precision = setup.phi_inverse_class.evaluate(10.0 ** rho)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
priors

The prior range on each power-spectrum amplitude.

  • Format: one [min, max] pair per non-empty \(k\) bin, in \(\rho_s = \log_{10}(\Delta^2_{21}/\mathrm{mK}^2)\).
  • Required: for any model including the EoR. Setup reports an error if the number of pairs does not match the number of bins.
uniform_priors

Selects bins whose prior is uniform in linear, rather than logarithmic, power.

  • Format: one 0 or 1 per bin.
  • Default: all 0, logarithmic.
  • Note: the sampler still works in \(\rho_s\); a Jacobian correction is added for the selected bins.

docs.title: Running inference
docs.text: With setup complete, BayesEoR explores the power-spectrum posterior with MultiNest, an implementation of nested sampling that allows simultaneous posterior exploration and Bayesian-evidence evaluation. Each likelihood call is a single marginalised likelihood evaluation, so the sampler only ever sees the power-spectrum amplitudes.

docs.title: Choosing the model
docs.text:
model selects which components are fitted. It describes the inference model, not the contents of the data, so the same dataset can be analysed with each.

eor+fg

The joint model, and the default.

  • Operator: \([\mathbf T_{21}\ \ \mathbf T'_{\rm FG}]\).
  • Sampled: the power-spectrum amplitudes, with MultiNest.
eor

The EoR alone.

  • Operator: \(\mathbf T_{21}\).
  • Sampled: the power-spectrum amplitudes, with MultiNest.
  • Note: foreground settings are ignored, and foreground_kl_path is rejected.
fg

The foregrounds alone, as the null hypothesis for model comparison.

  • Operator: \(\mathbf T'_{\rm FG}\), physical or reduced.
  • Sampled: nothing. The evidence and MAP coefficients are evaluated in one solve; see foreground-only evidence.
  • Note: priors and fov_eor are not needed.

Use a separate output directory for each model, so their results and metadata are kept apart.

docs.title: Nested sampling
docs.text:
run_nestedsampling runs MultiNest on a completed setup, or evaluates the foreground-only evidence directly when there is nothing to sample.

MathsCode

With the coefficients marginalised, the remaining posterior and evidence are

\[ P(\boldsymbol\rho\mid\boldsymbol d,\mathcal M) =\frac{\mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol\rho,\mathcal M)\, \pi(\boldsymbol\rho\mid\mathcal M)}{\mathcal Z_{\mathcal M}}, \qquad \mathcal Z_{\mathcal M} =\int\mathcal L(\boldsymbol d\mid\boldsymbol\rho,\mathcal M)\, \pi(\boldsymbol\rho\mid\mathcal M)\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol\rho. \]

Comparing \(\mathcal Z\) between the joint and foreground-only models quantifies the support for a 21-cm signal. Applying the same comparison to signal-free data tests whether the EoR component is absorbing unmodelled foreground structure instead.

from bayeseor_jax import BayesEoRParser, run_setup, run_nestedsampling

config = BayesEoRParser().parse_args(["--config", "config.yaml"])
setup = run_setup(config)
summary = run_nestedsampling(
    setup,
    out_dir=f"{config.output_dir}/multinest",
    random_key=config.random_key,
    n_live_scale_factor=config.n_live_scale_factor,
    resume=config.resume,
)

The sampler settings below are read from the configuration and passed to this call; the example script does this for you.

MultiNest needs both the native library and pymultinest, which the Conda environments install.

n_live_scale_factor

Sets the number of live points relative to the number of sampled parameters.

  • Default: 25, so live points \(= 25\,N_{\rm dim}\).
random_key

The sampler's random seed.

  • Default: 0.
resume

Continues an existing MultiNest run from output_dir.

  • Default: false.
  • Note: reports an error if no checkpoint files are found.
output_dir Where the sampler outputs and run metadata are written.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: MultiNest runs in a single process, while each likelihood evaluation uses the available JAX devices. On one CPU or GPU, the likelihood uses native JAX; across several GPUs, it uses JAXMg, with one process per GPU. To restrict a run to one GPU, set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0.

docs.title: Example script
docs.text:
The example script runs setup, and with --sample, nested sampling followed by a short posterior analysis:

python -m examples.eor.run
python -m examples.eor.run --sample

For scientific runs, use a dedicated configuration and output directory, and record the live-point count, seed and stopping settings with each result.

docs.title: Bayesian forward model
docs.text: In order to rigorously separate the components of the measured visibilities, BayesEoR models each of them at its physical origin, predicting the visibilities that a given sky would produce for comparison with the data. This section describes how the 21-cm signal and the foregrounds are each modelled, and how both are mapped through the instrument into a single model for the measured visibilities.

docs.title: The interferometric measurement equation
docs.text:
At full fidelity, every direction on the sky and every frequency is propagated into the data through the continuous measurement equation, which relates each visibility to the sky brightness, \(I\), weighted by the primary beam, \(P\):

\[ V_{ij}( u,t) =\int_{\Omega_{ m vis}(t)} P(\hat{ oldsymbol s}, u)\, I(\hat{ oldsymbol s}, u,t)\, \exp\!\left[-2\pi i\, oldsymbol u_{ij}( u)\cdot\hat{ oldsymbol s} ight] \mathrm d\Omega. \]

BayesEoR's goal is to solve the inverse of this problem. However, parameterising the brightness of every direction on the sky at every frequency would quickly become computationally intractable, and would give no way to separate the foregrounds from the cosmological signal. BayesEoR instead describes each component in a basis suited to its physics, and maps both into the visibilities through linear operators:

\[ oldsymbol m = \mathbf T_{21}\, oldsymbol a + \mathbf T_{ m FG}\, oldsymbol q, \qquad oldsymbol d = oldsymbol m + oldsymbol n. \]

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• EoR model: the 21-cm signal, \(\boldsymbol a\), is described by Fourier coefficients on a three-dimensional grid, which expose its line-of-sight structure and connect directly to the power spectrum.
  • Foreground model: the foregrounds, \(\boldsymbol q\), are described by smooth spectral amplitudes in each pixel of a spherical image grid, out to the horizon if required.
  • KL Reduced Basis: a latent compression, rooted in this physics, can be used to reduce the model before inference.
  • Construction and execution: how the operators are built, stored and run.

docs.title: Construction and execution
docs.text: Setup turns a configuration and its data into the arrays used by the inference. It builds the forward operators described in the previous pages, saves them to disk, and precomputes the fixed matrix products needed by the likelihood. As this happens once, before sampling, a setup run is also a quick way to check a configuration.

docs.title: Setup flow
docs.text:
run_setup(config) performs the following steps without modifying config. Pass build_foreground_kl=True to construct a KL basis at the configured foreground_kl_path using the resolved physical model and noise; otherwise an existing basis is loaded unchanged:

  1. Load and prepare the visibility data.
  2. Resolve the model geometry: the image pixels, the Fourier grid and, when the EoR is included, its \(k\) bins.
  3. Build or reuse \(\mathbf T_{21}\) and \(\mathbf T_{\rm FG}\), or load a reduced basis, and assemble the joint operator, \(\mathbf T = [\mathbf T_{21}\ \ \mathbf T_{\rm FG}]\).
  4. Build the inverse noise covariance.
  5. Precompute the likelihood products.
  6. Construct the priors and the marginalised likelihood, and return a SetupResult ready for sampling.

Because the sky coefficients are marginalised analytically, the likelihood depends on the data and operators only through a few fixed matrix products, which are computed here once rather than at every sampler step. Their mathematical formulation is presented in analytical marginalisation.

docs.title: Saved arrays
docs.text:
Setup writes its arrays to array_save_directory, and reuses them on later runs where possible.

T_21.npy, T_fg.npy

The EoR and foreground operators.

  • Shape: \((N_{\rm d}, N_{21})\) and \((N_{\rm d}, N_{\rm FG})\).
  • Reuse: kept whenever present, unless clobber is set.
T.npy

The joint operator, assembled from the saved component columns.

  • Shape: \((N_{\rm d}, N_{21} + N_{\rm FG})\).
Ninv.npy

The inverse noise variance of each visibility.

  • Shape: \((N_{\rm d},)\).
  • Reuse: rebuilt whenever the noise model changes.
T_Ninv_T.npy, dbar.npy, d_ninv_d.npy

The likelihood products, \(\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\mathbf T\), \(\mathbf T^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\boldsymbol d\) and \(\boldsymbol d^\dagger\mathbf N^{-1}\boldsymbol d\).

  • Reuse: the first is rebuilt if T.npy or Ninv.npy change; the two data products are recomputed on every run.
array_save_directory

Where the arrays are written.

  • Default: ./matrices/.
clobber

Rebuilds every array instead of reusing it.

  • Default: false.

Warning

Reuse checks that the saved files exist and are consistent with each other, but not that they came from the same configuration. When the observation or model settings change, use a new array_save_directory or set clobber.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
The two expensive stages of setup run on different hardware.

Operator construction runs on CPU. The time-frequency blocks of each operator are divided between the JAX processes, which all write to the same file, so every process needs the same shared filesystem. Each process uses the CPUs available to it, respecting CPU affinity and Slurm's per-task count. The job launcher, not BayesEoR, is responsible for starting the processes and setting thread counts.

Likelihood products and inference run on the default JAX devices, normally GPUs. A single device uses native JAX; across several GPUs, JAXMg requires one Python process per GPU, with distributed JAX initialised before setup. The KL decomposition follows the same rule.

docs.title: Using the operators directly
docs.text:
The operators can also be built outside run_setup, either as arrays in memory or as saved files.

In memoryDisk-backed

T_21 and T_fg evaluate a supplied block of the operator and return a JAX array. They do not read files, choose hardware or apply priors, so they can be used inside compiled code.

import jax
from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import T_21, T_fg

# Inputs already selected for matching times, frequencies and baselines.
T21_block = jax.jit(T_21)(lmn_21, uvw_lambda, beam_21, pixel_area_sr, F_prime, F_z)
Tfg_block = jax.jit(T_fg)(lmn_fg, uvw_lambda, beam_fg, pixel_area_sr, Q)

Here lmn is (time, 3, pixel), uvw_lambda is (frequency, 3, baseline) and the beam is (time, frequency, pixel).

The _build_save functions evaluate the same operators on CPU in time-frequency blocks and return the paths of the saved matrices. Every participating process makes the same calls.

from bayeseor_jax.model.construction.operator_construction import (
    T_21_build_save, T_fg_build_save, assemble_joint_operator,
)

path_21 = T_21_build_save(
    lmn_21, uvw_lambda, beam_21, pixel_area_sr, F_prime, F_z,
    output_path="arrays/T_21.npy",
)
path_fg = T_fg_build_save(
    lmn_fg, uvw_lambda, beam_fg, pixel_area_sr, Q,
    output_path="arrays/T_fg.npy",
)
path_joint = assemble_joint_operator(path_21, path_fg, output_path="arrays/T.npy")

BuildMatrices provides the same methods, using its configured observation and model.

docs.title: EoR model
docs.text:
BayesEoR describes the cosmological 21-cm signal on a three-dimensional Fourier grid. Each coefficient belongs to a single spatial scale, giving the model an intrinsic link to the power spectrum we aim to recover, and exposing the line-of-sight structure that distinguishes the signal from spectrally smooth foregrounds.

The coefficients, \(\boldsymbol a\), are mapped to the visibilities by a sequence of linear operators, read from right to left:

\[ \boldsymbol m_{21} = \mathbf F^{-1}\,\mathbf P\,\mathbf F'\,\mathbf F_z\,\boldsymbol a \equiv \mathbf T_{21}\,\boldsymbol a. \]

docs.title: 1. Choose the Fourier modes
docs.text:
The coefficients are defined on a grid of transverse angular modes, \((u,v)\), and line-of-sight spectral modes, \(\eta\), the Fourier dual of frequency. This model grid is separate from the baselines sampled by the instrument: it describes a local tangent plane, while the later propagation to visibilities uses the full three-dimensional sky directions.

MathsCode

A coefficient \(a_{he}\) belongs to transverse pair \((u_h,v_h)\) and spectral mode \(\eta_e\), the Fourier dual of observing frequency. The usual spacings are the reciprocal model extents and bandwidth:

\[ \Delta u=\Theta_l^{-1},\qquad \Delta v=\Theta_m^{-1},\qquad \Delta\eta=B^{-1}. \]

The transverse monopole \((u,v)=(0,0)\) and the \(\eta=0\) plane are excluded, leaving

\[ N_{21,\mathrm{param}}=(N_uN_v-1)(N_\eta-1). \]

When flattened, coefficients are ordered by transverse mode, with \(\eta\) varying fastest.

build_fourier_geometry takes grid sizes and spacings, and returns the retained coordinates and integration weights. This example uses eight transverse pairs and three spectral modes.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from bayeseor_jax.model.cosmology.fourier_geometry import build_fourier_geometry

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
frequencies_hz = 159e6 + jnp.arange(4) * 200e3
bandwidth_hz = 4 * 200e3
angular_extent_rad = jnp.deg2rad(20.0)
grid = build_fourier_geometry(
    n_u=3, n_v=3, n_eta=4,
    du=float(1 / angular_extent_rad),
    dv=float(1 / angular_extent_rad),
    d_eta=1 / bandwidth_hz,
)
assert grid.uv.shape == (2, 8)
assert grid.eta.shape == (3,)

Normal setup derives the transverse spacings from the pixel-padded model footprint and can infer suitable grid sizes from the observation. The explicit sizes here are only for following the calculation.

docs.title: 2. Reconstruct the frequency dependence
docs.text:
At each transverse mode, the spectral Fourier operator, \(\mathbf F_z\), combines the spectral modes into the field at each observing frequency.

MathsCode \[ S_h(\nu_f)=\sum_e(F_z)_{fe}a_{he}, \qquad (F_z)_{fe}=\Delta\eta\, \exp[-2\pi i(\nu_f-\nu_{\rm ref})\eta_e]. \]

The configured builder uses the middle observing channel as \(\nu_{\rm ref}\). The factor \(\Delta\eta\) supplies the Fourier integration weight.

build_spectral_fourier_operator accepts spectral coordinates, frequency offsets in Hz and the spectral spacing. It returns a matrix shaped (n_frequency, n_eta_mode).

from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_spectral_fourier_operator

frequency_offsets_hz = frequencies_hz - frequencies_hz[len(frequencies_hz) // 2]
F_z = build_spectral_fourier_operator(
    grid.eta, frequency_offsets_hz, grid.d_eta,
)
# A single unit coefficient illustrates one basis response, not a simulated sky.
a = jnp.zeros((grid.uv.shape[1], grid.eta.size), dtype=jnp.complex128)
a = a.at[0, 0].set(1.0)
spectral_field = F_z @ a.T
assert spectral_field.shape == (4, 8)

docs.title: 3. Reconstruct brightness at the sky pixels
docs.text:
The transverse Fourier operator, \(\mathbf F'\), maps the angular modes onto the HEALPix pixels of the model field. Each coefficient contributes across the whole image, rather than to a single pixel. The transform uses the pixel directions at the reference integration, and the same celestial pixels are then tracked as the Earth rotates.

MathsCode \[ I_{21,p}(\nu_f)=\sum_hF'_{ph}S_h(\nu_f), \qquad F'_{ph}=\Delta u\,\Delta v\, \exp[-2\pi i(u_hl_p+v_hm_p)]. \]

Here \((l_p,m_p)\) are the reference-time direction cosines of pixel \(p\). The pixel set contains the union of directions entering the cosmological field during the observation.

build_image_geometry selects and tracks the sky pixels. build_transverse_fourier_operator maps the Fourier grid onto their reference-time coordinates, returning (n_pixel, n_uv_mode).

from bayeseor_jax.model.observation.image_geometry import build_image_geometry
from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_transverse_fourier_operator

image = build_image_geometry(
    fov_eor=20.0, nside=16, n_t=1, d_t=10.0,
    jd_center=2461040.5,
)
# The shared geometry stores pixels on its foreground axis; select the EoR set.
selected = image.eor_fg_shared_axis
lmn = image.lmn_fg[:, :, selected]
az_za = image.az_za_fg[:, :, selected]
lm_reference = lmn[image.time_ind_center, :2, :]
F_prime = build_transverse_fourier_operator(
    grid.uv, lm_reference, grid.du * grid.dv,
)
brightness = spectral_field @ F_prime.T
assert brightness.shape == (4, lmn.shape[-1])

The small HEALPix resolution keeps this demonstration lightweight. For an analysis, setup checks the required resolution against the sampled baselines and frequencies.

docs.title: 4. Weight each pixel by the primary beam
docs.text:
The primary beam, \(\mathbf P\), weights each pixel by its direction and frequency, with zero response at and below the horizon. See the primary beam for the supported models.

MathsCode \[ I^{\rm beam}_{tfp}=P_{tfp}\,I_{21,p}(\nu_f). \]

The beam operator is diagonal in image space. We apply its weights directly rather than constructing a dense diagonal matrix.

Beam_Model.get_beam_vals takes azimuth/zenith-angle coordinates and frequencies in Hz. Its output order is (frequency, time, pixel); the visibility operator expects (time, frequency, pixel).

from bayeseor_jax.model.instrument.beam import Beam_Model

beam_model = Beam_Model(beam_type="airy", diam=14.2)
beam = beam_model.get_beam_vals(az_za, frequencies_hz).transpose(1, 0, 2)
beam_weighted_brightness = beam * brightness[None, :, :]
assert beam_weighted_brightness.shape == (1, 4, lmn.shape[-1])

docs.title: 5. Add each pixel's contribution to the visibilities
docs.text:
Finally, \(\mathbf F^{-1}\) applies the three-dimensional fringe response of each baseline and sums over the pixels, giving the cosmological visibilities. In the code, the beam and fringe are combined into a single operator, \(\mathbf R = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\), which already includes the pixel solid angle, so it must not be applied again.

MathsCode \[ \delta m_{21,tfbp} =\underbrace{\Delta\Omega\, e^{+2\pi i\boldsymbol u_b(\nu_f)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)} P_{tfp}}_{R_{tfbp}}\,I_{21,p}(\nu_f), \qquad m_{21,tfb}=\sum_p\delta m_{21,tfbp}. \]

Here \(\Delta\Omega\) is the pixel solid angle and \(\boldsymbol u_b\) is the baseline in wavelengths. The positive fringe sign follows the code's ant2 - ant1 baseline convention. See build_sky_to_visibility_operator for the convention and units.

build_sky_to_visibility_operator combines sky directions, baselines in wavelengths, beam weights and pixel area into an array shaped (time, frequency, baseline, pixel).

from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_sky_to_visibility_operator

# Two opposite 10-m baselines, in the same topocentric frame as lmn.
baselines_m = jnp.array([[10.0, -10.0], [0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
uvw_lambda = frequencies_hz[:, None, None] / 299792458.0 * baselines_m
R = build_sky_to_visibility_operator(
    lmn, uvw_lambda, beam, image.pixel_area_sr,
)
# R already includes the beam: use intrinsic brightness here.
model_by_step = jnp.einsum("tfbp,fp->tfb", R, brightness)
assert model_by_step.shape == (1, 4, 2)

docs.title: 6. Put the steps together
docs.text:
Combining these gives \(\mathbf T_{21}\), whose columns describe how each Fourier coefficient contributes to every visibility. Applying it to \(\boldsymbol a\) gives the same result as following the steps above.

MathsCode

Combining the steps, the contribution of every coefficient \(a_{he}\) to the visibility measured by baseline \(b\) at frequency \(\nu_f\) and time \(t\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} m_{21,tfb} ={}& \sum_{h,e}\sum_{p} \Delta\Omega\, \exp\!\left[+2\pi i\,\boldsymbol u_b(\nu_f)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)\right] P_{tfp} \\ &\times \Delta u\,\Delta v\, \exp\!\left[-2\pi i\,(u_h l_p + v_h m_p)\right] \\ &\times \Delta\eta\, \exp\!\left[-2\pi i\,(\nu_f-\nu_{\rm ref})\,\eta_e\right] a_{he}. \end{aligned} \]

Stacking over times, frequencies and baselines gives \(\boldsymbol m_{21} = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\mathbf F'\mathbf F_z\boldsymbol a \equiv \mathbf T_{21}\boldsymbol a\). Rows are ordered by time, frequency and baseline, with baseline varying fastest; columns are ordered by transverse mode, then spectral mode.

build_T_21_core contracts the three supplied operators. T_21 provides the same calculation while constructing the beam-weighted response from geometry arrays.

import numpy as np
from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_T_21_core

T = build_T_21_core(R, F_prime, F_z)
model = T @ a.reshape(-1)
assert T.shape == (8, 24)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    model, model_by_step.reshape(-1), rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-15,
)

For larger calculations, T_21_build_save evaluates CPU time-frequency blocks and saves T_21.npy. The construction workflow changes how this operator is built and stored, not its mathematical definition.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Setup builds the Fourier grid from the observation and these settings. A larger field of view or Fourier grid adds coefficients to the model, increasing the memory and computation required.

fov_eor

The full angular diameter of the EoR model field.

  • Default: 10.
  • Units: degrees.
  • Note: the model covers every pixel that enters this field during the observation.
n_u_eor, n_v_eor

The number of transverse modes along \(u\) and \(v\).

  • Default: inferred, so the grid covers the longest baseline at the highest frequency, plus half the beam's aperture width on each side.
  • Note: smaller values are kept, with a warning.
du_eor, dv_eor

The transverse mode spacings.

  • Default: the reciprocal of the model field's angular extent along each axis.
  • Units: inverse radians.
  • Note: values that differ from the default by more than 5% produce a warning.
n_eta

The number of line-of-sight modes.

  • Default: n_freq.
nside

The HEALPix resolution of the image grid, shared with the foreground model.

  • Default: inferred from the longest baseline and highest frequency.
  • Note: lower values are kept, with a warning.

See the examples for complete, commented configurations.

docs.title: Foreground model
docs.text:
BayesEoR describes the foregrounds directly on the sky, as smooth spectra in each pixel of a spherical HEALPix grid. Working on the sphere, rather than a tangent plane, lets the model extend all the way to the horizon, while the spectral smoothness of the foregrounds is what separates them from the 21-cm signal.

The amplitudes, \(\boldsymbol q\), are mapped to the visibilities by a sequence of linear operators, read from right to left:

\[ \boldsymbol m_{\rm FG} = \mathbf F^{-1}\,\mathbf P\,\mathbf Q_z\,\boldsymbol q \equiv \mathbf T_{\rm FG}\,\boldsymbol q. \]

docs.title: 1. Choose the sky pixels
docs.text:
The model covers every celestial pixel that enters the foreground field of view during the observation, and tracks its direction relative to the instrument at each integration. Each pixel carries its own spectral amplitudes, so a wider field adds coefficients without changing the construction.

MathsCode

For spectral component \(g\), collect the amplitudes of all selected pixels into

\[ \boldsymbol q_g=(q_{g,1},\ldots,q_{g,N_{\rm pix}})^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \boldsymbol q=(\boldsymbol q_0^{\mathsf T},\ldots, \boldsymbol q_{N_\beta}^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}. \]

The configured spectral model has a constant component and one component per power-law index, giving

\[ N_{\rm FG,param}=(1+N_\beta)N_{\rm pix}. \]

Pixel identities stay fixed on the celestial sky, but their topocentric directions \(\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)=(l_p(t),m_p(t),n_p(t))\) change with observing time.

build_image_geometry takes field extents, HEALPix resolution, telescope location and observing times. It returns the pixel directions, beam coordinates and pixel solid angle.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from bayeseor_jax.model.observation.image_geometry import build_image_geometry

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
frequencies_hz = 159e6 + jnp.arange(4) * 200e3
image = build_image_geometry(
    fov_eor=20.0, fov_fg=180.0, nside=8,
    n_t=2, d_t=10.0, jd_center=2461040.5,
)
lmn = image.lmn_fg
az_za = image.az_za_fg
n_pixel = lmn.shape[-1]
assert lmn.shape == (2, 3, n_pixel)

The helper constructs shared geometry for both sky components; here we use only its foreground pixels. The low resolution keeps the example lightweight, not suitable for production analysis. Normal setup checks the resolution against the observation.

docs.title: 2. Reconstruct each pixel's spectrum
docs.text:
The spectral operator, \(\mathbf Q_z\), turns each pixel's amplitudes into its brightness at every observing frequency. The spectrum is a constant plus a set of power laws, whose slopes are shared across the sky and whose amplitudes are free in each pixel.

MathsCode \[ I_{{\rm FG},p}(\nu_f)=\sum_g Q_{fg}q_{g,p}, \qquad Q_{f0}=1,\quad Q_{fg}=\left(\frac{\nu_f}{\nu_0}\right)^{-\beta_g}\quad(g>0). \]

The full spectral operator is \(\mathbf Q_z=\mathbf Q\otimes\mathbf I_{N_{\rm pix}}\) with component-major coefficient ordering. The builder uses the first observing channel as \(\nu_0\).

build_foreground_spectral_operator takes frequencies in MHz, a reference frequency and signed power-law exponents. It returns (n_frequency, n_component).

from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_foreground_spectral_operator

frequencies_mhz = frequencies_hz / 1e6
Q = build_foreground_spectral_operator(
    frequencies_mhz,
    reference_frequency_mhz=float(frequencies_mhz[0]),
    spectral_indices=(-2.63, -2.82),
)
# Excite one pixel's first power-law component to follow its basis response.
q = jnp.zeros((Q.shape[1], n_pixel), dtype=jnp.float64)
pixel = int(jnp.argmax(lmn[image.time_ind_center, 2, :]))
q = q.at[1, pixel].set(1.0)
brightness = Q @ q
assert Q.shape == (4, 3)
assert brightness.shape == (4, n_pixel)

This unit amplitude illustrates a basis response, not a realistic foreground realisation. The operator preserves the supplied brightness units. In run configuration, beta_fg: [2.63, 2.82] uses positive slopes; the builder negates them before calling this function.

docs.title: 3. Weight the brightness by the primary beam
docs.text:
The primary beam, \(\mathbf P\), weights each pixel by its direction and frequency. Its response is zero at and below the horizon, so pixels stop contributing as they set. See the primary beam for the supported models.

MathsCode \[ I^{\rm beam}_{{\rm FG},tfp} =P_{tfp}I_{{\rm FG},p}(\nu_f). \]

The weights act independently on each image pixel. There is no need to allocate a dense diagonal beam matrix.

Beam_Model.get_beam_vals accepts azimuth/zenith-angle coordinates and frequencies in Hz. Reorder its (frequency, time, pixel) output for the forward operators.

from bayeseor_jax.model.instrument.beam import Beam_Model

beam_model = Beam_Model(beam_type="airy", diam=14.2)
beam = beam_model.get_beam_vals(az_za, frequencies_hz).transpose(1, 0, 2)
beam_weighted_brightness = beam * brightness[None, :, :]
assert beam_weighted_brightness.shape == (2, 4, n_pixel)
assert bool(jnp.all(beam[jnp.broadcast_to(
    az_za[:, 1:2, :] >= jnp.pi / 2, beam.shape,
)] == 0))

See instrument configuration for the other analytic profiles and interpolated beam inputs.

docs.title: 4. Add the pixel contributions to each visibility
docs.text:
Finally, \(\mathbf F^{-1}\) applies the full three-dimensional fringe response of each baseline and sums over the pixels. Keeping the \(w\) term retains the wide-field geometry, including directions close to the horizon. As in the EoR model, the beam and fringe are combined in the code into \(\mathbf R = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\), which already includes the pixel solid angle.

MathsCode \[ \delta m_{{\rm FG},tfbp} =\underbrace{\Delta\Omega\, e^{+2\pi i\boldsymbol u_b(\nu_f)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)} P_{tfp}}_{R_{tfbp}}I_{{\rm FG},p}(\nu_f), \qquad m_{{\rm FG},tfb}=\sum_p\delta m_{{\rm FG},tfbp}. \]

Baselines \(\boldsymbol u_b\) are expressed in wavelengths. The positive fringe sign follows the code's ant2 - ant1 convention, as implemented in build_sky_to_visibility_operator.

build_sky_to_visibility_operator returns the beam-weighted response with shape (time, frequency, baseline, pixel).

from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_sky_to_visibility_operator

baselines_m = jnp.array([[10.0, -10.0], [0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
uvw_lambda = frequencies_hz[:, None, None] / 299792458.0 * baselines_m
R = build_sky_to_visibility_operator(
    lmn, uvw_lambda, beam, image.pixel_area_sr,
)
# Use intrinsic brightness because R already applies the beam.
model_by_step = jnp.einsum("tfbp,fp->tfb", R, brightness)
assert model_by_step.shape == (2, 4, 2)

docs.title: 5. Put the steps together
docs.text:
Combining these gives \(\mathbf T_{\rm FG}\), whose columns describe how each spectral amplitude in each pixel contributes to every visibility.

MathsCode

Combining the steps, the contribution of every amplitude \(q_{g,p}\) to the visibility measured by baseline \(b\) at frequency \(\nu_f\) and time \(t\) is

\[ m_{{\rm FG},tfb} = \sum_{p} \Delta\Omega\, \exp\!\left[+2\pi i\,\boldsymbol u_b(\nu_f)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol s}_p(t)\right] P_{tfp} \left[q_{0,p} + \sum_{g\geq1} q_{g,p} \left(\frac{\nu_f}{\nu_0}\right)^{-\beta_g}\right]. \]

Stacking over times, frequencies and baselines gives \(\boldsymbol m_{\rm FG} = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf P\mathbf Q_z\boldsymbol q \equiv \mathbf T_{\rm FG}\boldsymbol q\). Rows are ordered by time, frequency and baseline, with baseline varying fastest; columns are ordered by spectral component, then pixel.

build_T_fg_core combines the response and spectral factors. T_fg also constructs the response directly from the supplied geometry and beam arrays.

import numpy as np
from bayeseor_jax.model.operators import build_T_fg_core

T = build_T_fg_core(R, Q)
model = T @ q.reshape(-1)
assert T.shape == (16, 3 * n_pixel)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    model, model_by_step.reshape(-1), rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-15,
)

For disk-backed construction, T_fg_build_save evaluates the same mapping in CPU time-frequency blocks and writes T_fg.npy. See the construction workflow for execution and storage.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
fov_fg

The full angular diameter of the foreground model field.

  • Default: fov_eor.
  • Units: degrees.
  • Note: bright foregrounds remain visible through the beam sidelobes, so this is usually larger than fov_eor. Use 180 to model the full sky to the horizon.
beta_fg

The power-law spectral indices, \(\beta_g\), shared across the sky.

  • Default: [2.63, 2.82], for Galactic synchrotron and extragalactic sources.
  • Sign: positive values give spectra falling as \((\nu/\nu_0)^{-\beta_g}\).
  • Note: together with the constant term, this sets the number of spectral components per pixel, \(1 + N_\beta\).
nside The HEALPix resolution, shared with the EoR model.

See the 21-cm and foregrounds example for a complete, commented configuration.

docs.title: KL Reduced Basis
docs.text:
The Karhunen–Loève (KL) reduced basis is a general compression for any linear model component with a Gaussian prior, equivalent to an optimal low-rank approximation of a Bayesian linear inverse problem (Spantini et al. 2015). It propagates the component's physically motivated structure through to its prior-predictive covariance in visibility space, and represents that covariance in an orthogonal basis ordered by how far each mode rises above the noise. Modes the data cannot distinguish from noise are then discarded.

For a component \(\boldsymbol m = \mathbf T\boldsymbol x\) with prior \(\boldsymbol x \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol 0, \mathbf\Sigma)\), the compression proceeds as

\[ \mathbf T \ \longrightarrow\ \mathbf A=\mathbf N^{-1/2}\mathbf T\,\mathbf\Sigma^{1/2} \ \longrightarrow\ (\mathbf U,\mathbf S) \ \longrightarrow\ \mathbf T_r . \]

Because the coefficients are marginalised analytically, the inference depends only on the uncertainty they induce in the visibilities, \(\mathbf C = \mathbf T\mathbf\Sigma\mathbf T^\dagger\), not on the coefficients themselves. Any basis spanning \(\mathbf C\) is therefore equivalent, and the reduced operator, \(\mathbf T_r\), replaces \(\mathbf T\) in the same visibility space with far fewer columns.

The pipeline currently applies this to the foreground model, whose physical basis is the largest. The same construction could be applied to the EoR model independently within each \(k\) bin, keeping the power-spectrum amplitudes as sampled parameters.

docs.title: 1. Weight the mapping by prior and noise
docs.text:
Each coefficient is scaled by its prior standard deviation, and each visibility by its inverse noise RMS, so that the operator's response is measured relative to the noise.

MathsCode \[ \mathbf A=\mathbf N^{-1/2}\mathbf T\,\mathbf\Sigma^{1/2}, \qquad \mathbf C_w = \mathbf N^{-1/2}\mathbf C\,\mathbf N^{-1/2} = \mathbf A\mathbf A^\dagger. \]

\(\mathbf C_w\) is the prior-predictive covariance in noise-whitened visibility space. For diagonal priors and noise, each column of \(\mathbf T\) is multiplied by its prior standard deviation and each row divided by its noise RMS.

weight_foreground_operator applies these factors to an existing operator, and T_fg_weighted constructs and weights a visibility block directly.

For a full analysis, T_fg_weighted_build_save builds \(\mathbf A\) in CPU blocks and saves it as A_fg.npy, without first saving the unweighted operator.

docs.title: 2. Decompose the weighted operator
docs.text:
A singular-value decomposition of \(\mathbf A\) gives an orthonormal set of visibility-space modes, each with a variance measured relative to the noise.

MathsCode \[ \mathbf A=\mathbf U\mathbf S\mathbf V^\dagger, \qquad \mathbf C_w = \mathbf U\mathbf S^2\mathbf U^\dagger. \]

The columns of \(\mathbf U\) are the KL modes, and \(\lambda_i = s_i^2\) is the prior-predictive variance of each relative to the noise. An eigendecomposition of \(\mathbf C_w\) gives the same modes; the operator form is smaller when there are fewer coefficients than visibilities. The number of modes is bounded by

\[ r \leq \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf C) \leq \min(N_{\rm d}, N_{\rm param}), \]

and keeping the largest modes minimises the discarded whitened variance for any given rank, which is the sense in which the basis is statistically optimal.

T_fg_svd_build_save performs the decomposition, truncation and rescaling of steps 2 to 4 in one call. It uses an exact, thin SVD of \(\mathbf A\):

  • CPU: native JAX on a single device. \(\mathbf A\), \(\mathbf U\) and the workspace must fit in RAM.
  • GPU: distributed with JAXMg, with one process per GPU and shared storage.

docs.title: 3. Choose the retained rank
docs.text:
The modes are truncated once the variance left over is a small fraction of the noise, so the reduced basis preserves the component's uncertainty to that level.

MathsCode

With the singular values ordered from largest to smallest, keep the smallest \(r\) satisfying

\[ \epsilon_{\rm RMS}(r) =\left[\frac{1}{N_{\rm d}}\sum_{i>r}s_i^2\right]^{1/2} \leq f. \]

The default \(f = 0.1\) limits the discarded prior-predictive RMS, averaged over the visibilities, to ten per cent of the noise RMS. It is not a bound on every individual visibility.

select_foreground_rank implements this criterion, and is called by T_fg_svd_build_save through its f argument.

docs.title: 4. Restore visibility units
docs.text:
The retained modes are un-whitened, keeping the prior absorbed into them, to give the reduced operator.

MathsCode \[ \mathbf T_r=\mathbf N^{1/2}\mathbf U_r\mathbf S_r, \qquad \boldsymbol m^{(r)}=\mathbf T_r\boldsymbol z, \qquad \boldsymbol z \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol 0, \mathbf I_r). \]

The latent coefficients, \(\boldsymbol z\), have a standard-normal prior by construction, and the retained covariance is \(\mathbf C^{(r)}=\mathbf T_r\mathbf T_r^\dagger\).

from bayeseor_jax import T_fg_svd_build_save

reduced_path = T_fg_svd_build_save(
    "arrays/A_fg.npy",
    "arrays/Ninv.npy",
    output_path="arrays/T_fg_reduced.npy",
    f=0.1,
)

Ninv.npy must be the inverse noise used to build \(\mathbf A\). The routine also saves the singular values, T_fg_reduced.singular_values.npy, and the truncation diagnostics, T_fg_reduced.svd.json.

docs.title: Building through setup
docs.text:
To construct the basis and likelihood in one pipeline call, set foreground_kl_path in the configuration and run:

from bayeseor_jax import run_setup

setup = run_setup(config, build_foreground_kl=True, kl_f=0.1)

Setup resolves the observation once, saves the prior- and noise-weighted A_fg.npy, and calls T_fg_svd_build_save to save the reduced operator and its diagnostics. Joint assembly then uses its standard-normal latent prior. This explicitly rebuilds the KL basis; omit build_foreground_kl to reuse an existing basis for the same observation, noise and foreground prior.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
foreground_kl_path

A saved reduced operator, used in place of the physical foreground model.

  • Effect: its columns are used with a unit prior. By default setup loads the saved basis unchanged; foreground_prior_std_mk is not applied again.
  • Requires: model: fg or model: eor+fg.
  • Note: the operator must match the observation, visibility ordering and foreground prior it was built from. Shape checks alone cannot confirm this.

See execution for the CPU and distributed-GPU workflow.
